## Preface

The destruction, desecration and plunder of temples is millennial old long rupture that has wounded and destroyed Bharat and has had devastating impact on its socio-economic conditions. It started with Greek invasion, achieved its threshold during the Mughal invasion and their occupation and institutionalized by British and other European invaders who focused extensively on plundering the wealth of this country consigned and consolidated within the temples to serve humanity. The plunder did not stop even after transfer of power in 1947. Except Hindus everyone got independence on 15 August 1947. Hindus are till date struggling to free their temples from the clutches of secular government which took over the power in 1947, after transfer of power.

On 22 April 2020, the Tamil Nadu government issued a circular asking 47 temples under the control of the state government to contribute a total amount of Rs 10 crore of their surplus to the Chief Minister's Relief Fund. (Tamil Nadu: Madras HC intervenes, govt withdraws order asking only Hindu temples to pay Rs 10 crores to CM's Coronavirus relief fund, 5 May 2020, Opindia.com) The Tamil Nadu government order is since reversed after Hindus moved the court.

During the lockdown due to Chinese virus, we came across various new and unique issues. But one old issue came up again during lock down and was extremely annoying i.e., "demand by few Hindus to appropriate Temple Gold by the government" Neither the Central government in Bharat nor any of the state governments in the country, since the outbreak of Chinese Virus, had mentioned any shortage of funds. But few "individuals, organisations and political parties" within Bharat do not want to miss any chance to loot temple of its built-up resources over period of time by devotees.

After transfer of power in 1947, communists in the disguise of secularists had withheld renovation or reconstruction of any temples. Restoration of Somnath Mandir stands out as a case in point. There are enough literature documenting Jawaharlal Nehru's opposition to the restoration of temple. I will just cite two examples here.

First: In the early months of 1951, just few weeks before the temple inauguration, at the end of a Cabinet meeting, Nehru called K M Munshi and said: "I don't like your trying to restore Somnath. It is Hindu revivalism."

Second: When the then president of India, Rajendra Prasad, was invited to inaugurate the temple, Nehru shot him a letter, admonishing, "I confess that I do not like the idea of your associating yourself with a spectacular opening of the Somnath Temple.

Incidentally, on 11 May 1951, Rajendra Prasad, while presiding over the opening ceremony of the temple, said: "Somnath was the symbol of economic and spiritual prosperity of ancient India." (70 Years Ago Today The Somnath Temple Was Restored 11 May, 1951, Swarajyamag.com)

Over the period, the buck did not stop with opposing renovation or restoration of

<!-- page 5 -->

temples. Instead of protecting the temple assets; theft and pilferage of ancient statues created and consecrated through age-old time-tested sciences, stealing, and smuggling of statues was promoted as a cultural industry. It is so bad that, on 9 November 2011, the Madras High Court warned that the Tamil Nadu Director-General of Police (DGP) would face consequences if its directives in the idol's theft cases were not adhered to in letter and spirit. (Idol Theft Cases: What Made Madras High Court Warn The Tamil Nadu Police Chief by M R Subramani, 11 November 2019, swarajyamag.com)

With all this in a synchronised manner steps were taken to alienate Hindus from temples through films, literature, jokes, cartoons, activism etc. Let me cite few examples from Urduwood:

- Suhaag (1979): The villain, demands to see murder executed on Navratri inside a mandir.
- Pannah (1992): When butchers wanted to sacrifice you in Kali mandir, none of your (Hindu) gods rescues you. Only and only Joseph did.
- Khuda Gawah (1992): Heroine is sings "Khuda Gawah" for a pathan in a mandir in front of Bhagwan Krishna murty.
- Kanoon (1994): Hero enters the temple with shoes, swears revenge on Bhagwan Shiv, calls him "zaalim" who has done many "sitam" on his devotees. Temple shown as a haunted-looking abandoned place with cobwebs and snakes all over. Temple bells used for adding to the eerie atmosphere.
- Haider (2014): Martand Temple (Sun Temple) of Kashmir is shown as the den of devil.
- Wazir (2016): Hindu protagonists stuck in complex problems often find direction inside a mosque. In this movie a Pandit father finds solace and clarity following the death of his daughter.
- Thank God (2022): Among hero's "sins", CG (a modern-day Chitragupta) recounts how the realtor spent money feeding laddoos to Hanumanji instead of using that money to feed beggars outside the temple. "Even Hanumanji doesn't like how you pour water, stick coins and smear vermillion on him. Enough," CG lectures the Hindu audience, and adds, "To please stones, you murdered flowers." This scene essentially conveys the message that temples are corrupt, vitiated places where stones (murtis of Hindu deities) are given preference over real human beings out of superstition and which are patronised by the worst of the human beings.
- Kisi Ka Bhai Kisi Ki Jaan (2023): Vulgar song shot in front of a mandir

The sum effect of this kind of malicious propaganda that defames Hindu mandir and

imbibe guilt has resulted in Hindus feeling ashamed of their temples and being permissive about the loot of their own temples.

At this pace Hindus will be brainwashed perpetually, enough to demand destruction of their own temples (some already do it). Before this catastrophe hits upon we Hindus, I decided to delve and write a book, "Temple Economics" Or 'Arthavyavastha of Mandirs' with an attempt to document this journey of

- brainwashing of Hindu minds against their own temple,
- importance of 'Temple Economics' in Bharat and way forward.

By the time I ended up writing, I ended up with series of books on this topic.

The first two volumes in the series are –

Volume I: Arthvyavasta of Mandir/ Temple Economics. It explains, traces the antiquity, and ebb & flow of temple economics.

Volume II: Mandiron ke liye Ek Dashak/ A Decade For Mandirs. Writing and reading is not going to solve the problem of mandirs. One must take concrete steps on the ground for that. This volume covers those concrete steps.

I am hopeful and optimistic that after reading this series, Hindus will understand the crucial role of temples in ensuring survival of Hindu/ Bharatiya civilisation and they will become active to support and protect temples; take charge of temples as well as counter the narrative of annihilation being built of ancient surviving civilization against all odds through ages.

I am targeting to release other two volumes in the series by the year end, provided I get financial support for the same.

I also wanted to cover temples outside Bharat but again constraint of time and money stopped me from doing so.

I will also like to make it clear that if you are looking to read about dharma or spirituality, then this is not the book for you. But if you want to attain moksha by dedicating yourself to the cause of mandirs, then these two volumes are written for you and you only.

These volumes may not meet the criteria of regular books on many counts. For example, the format of acknowledging the source. The name of the work comes first and the name of the author later. The idea being that the work is bigger than the individual. This is the Hindu way.

The word Dharma is written as Dharm, Rama as Ram and so and so forth. This is the Hindu way.

Will we accept if our name is twisted? If not, then why do we accept twisted names of our Devi, Devtas. Those who give argument of English grammar to them my answer is simple; do not use a language whose grammar is flawed or correct the grammar. For a flawed language I will not change name of our Devi, Devata. This is the Hindu way.

<!-- page 6 -->

There is a word Urduwood used in the book. For the uninitiated it is blend of Urdu + Bollywood, representing movie industry based in Mumbai for their imposition of Urdu words and their bias against Hindus and Hindutava.

The book has case studies. It means the point raised in the case study should be discussed and deliberated upon.

Within chapter the source is mentioned, while at the end of the chapter some recommended reading and watch list is given. It does not mean I endorse other works of the author/video maker whose work I have recommended. The source mentioned are not recommended reading, they are just the source.

Some information will not be up to date, because mandirs and related aspects are being attacked at such a speed that it is almost impossible to keep pace.

Some classifications like sects, religious institutions etc. have been done for ease of presentation. Idea is not to hurt anyone's sentiments or twist the facts. I will be very happy to be corrected.

Protection of the mandir is protection of Hindu civilisation and Bharat. Time has come for Hindus to snatch their mandirs from the claws of secular government as well as invaders. I have mentioned 'Transfer of Power in 1947'. This is in the context of mandirs. Mandirs did not get their freedom. For mandirs, it was just transfer of power in 1947 and not independence.

This is a workbook for those who want to work for mandir.

It is said that every good work faces obstacles. Writing this book was no different. People tried to grab my ancestral property and it not only delayed the book but had a cascading impact on many things including financial. Friends and administration helped me overcome this and I remain obliged to them.

Those who want to share their views, can communicate with me on templeeconomics@gmail.com This is the Hindu way.

There are many things in the books which will upset many people. Those who want to abuse can do so on X @authorsandeep. This is the secular way.

Wishing you a happy reading.

- Sandeep Singh

## Economic impact of pilgrimage in Jammu and Kashmir

| Place | Income through Pilgrimage Tourism at Current Prices |
|---|---|
| Amarnath Yatra | ₹ 6,24,05,28,470 |
| Mata Vaishnov Devi | ₹ 72,65,87,82,000 |
| Shiv Khori | ₹ 13,70,76,02,000 |
| Hemis Gompa | ₹ 1,32,07,60,000 |

- In the accommodation and food sectors tourism industry creates about 40,000 full time and part time jobs in Jammu and Kashmir.
- During peak seasons about 50,000 people work in the accommodation and food sector and about 10,000 people work as photographers and as workers in various photo-processing studios in the state at various tourist spots.
- About 2,00,000 people are working in the transportation sector.
- In Kashmir division only there are 65,236 taxies, busses and cars which work in the tourism sector.
- About 523 people work as tour operators who provide sightseeing services. And many tour operators work on part time basis mainly because of the huge rush during the peak season.
- The handmade shawls and wood carving products are very popular among the tourists and about 35,000 people work in these businesses.
- Apart from these about 15,000 people deal in tea/coffee, mineral water, sunglasses and other small vendors businesses.
- Construction in Jammu and Kashmir from the last 10 years or so is becoming a booming business and about 60,000 people work in this sector and earn their living.
- Approximately 1,00,000 people work in pilgrimage tourism sector out of which about 65% work on full time basis and 35% work at least nine months a year, according to the appropriate tourism estimates.
- Apart from that about 45,000 people work indirectly in the tourism related businesses like poultry farmers, vegetable and flower producers, fish sellers and landlords.

(Economic Analysis of tourism industry in Jammu and Kashmir, with special reference to pilgrimage tourism. A Thesis Submitted to Jiwaji University, Gwalior for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy In Economics, 2018 by Ishfaq Ahmad Ganai)

# 1. Temple or Mandir, Economics or Arthashastra !

*To understand the nuances of a word in its entirety, it is essential to understand the host culture. Language, both reflects and shapes, a culture's thought process owing to its deep structures and categories. The unique experiences of different cultures are not always interchangeable. Many cultural artifacts have no equivalent in other cultures, and to force such artifacts into Western templates results in distortions. This too is a kind of colonization and cultural conquest. Therefore, certain words used to refer to those experiences must remain intact.*

\- Sanskrit Non-Translatables, 2020 by
Rajiv Malhotra & Satyanarayana Dasa Babaji, Amaryllis

There is a world of a difference between 'Temple Economics' and 'Mandir based Arthavyavastha'. I have used the term Temple Economics only to make it easier for the readers to grasp the issue. It is important to take cognizant of the difference and for that let us understand the difference between the words 'Temple and Mandir', and 'Economics and Arthashastra'.

### Temple or Mandir?

To quote Jagadguru Kanchi Kaamakoti Sankaracharya Swami on mandirs: "Our temples are not organised as places for meditation, nor for congregational worship. The purpose of a temple is different. We enjoy the good things in life such as house, food, clothing, ornaments, music, dance, etc. We pay a tribute in the form of taxes to the king-now the Government-for making it possible for us to enjoy them by giving us their protection. The king-protector is provided with a place and other paraphernalia of royalty. Even as we render homage to the king for the enjoyment of these things, we are bound to render our gratitude to God who has primarily given us the good things of life. We offer a part of these good things as a token of our gratitude to Him in the temple. We first offer to Him all that He has given us, in the shape of food, clothing, jewels, music, flowers, light, incense, etc., with the grateful consciousness that they are His gifts to us; and we receive them back from Him as His prasaada. The temple is the place where these offerings are made on behalf of the collective community. Even if people do not go to the temple, it is enough if these offerings are made to God on behalf of the community. The duty of the people at the place is to see that these offerings are made in the proper manner. There are people who do not take their day's meal till the temple-bell announces that the offering to God of food for the day has been done. Then only do they take their meal as Prasaadam." According to the Gita if we enjoy these things without offering them first to the giver, it would tantamount to theft. (Temple Worship In Pre- Epic Period (Prior to 1000 B.C.) K. K. Menon, Temple in India, Vivekananda Kendra Patrika)

<!-- page 12 -->

4

We Hindus go to "Mandir", not to "Temple". A temple (derived from the Latin word templum) is a building reserved for religious or spiritual rituals and activities such as prayer and sacrifice. The word 'Temple' is used for buildings belonging to all faiths where a more specific term such as church, mosque or synagogue is not generally used in English. World recognises 'synagogue' as a place of worship while Jews have a population of less than two crores across the world. On the other hand, In Bharat which has eighty crore Hindus, the abode of their Bhagwan is called Temple, a generic word which also denotes the place of worship of ancient religions. Time has come to correct this anomaly and there is a valid reason for that.

Temple is place of worship; Mandir is abode of Bhagwan. Before a mandir is built, there are due ritualistic procedures to be undertaken like bhumi shodhana (cleansing the earth), vastu-puja, (worship of the ground divinities), bali-dana (making offerings to the attendant spirits), homa (fire-rituals), prathameshtika-nyasa (laying of the first brick), garbha-nyasa (womb-consecration), and so on. Unless these rituals are undertaken, the icon installed within the mandirs (sanctum) built by human will fall short of having consecrated divine presence.

Mandirs are consecrated according to the shastra (tradition/specific science/norm) by application of different proportionate measurements and standards. The mandirs have their own rhythm and grammar. The mandirs culture in Bharat is unique. It is intimately interwoven with the life of the people, both as individuals and society. It comprehends several aspects of community life, dharma, social, cultural, economic, educational and unifying aspects. As per Vastusilpakosa, "it utilises gainfully the energy, talent, skill and leisure of the members of the community". A mandir complex is comprehensive in the performance of various functions, utilities, forms and artifacts which pronounce their magnanimity and splendour.

**Names of Mandir:** Mandir is referred to by several names such as Alayam, Ambalam, Degul, Déul, Deva Mandiraya, Devalaya, Devagriha, Devatayatana Devasthana, Gudi, Kavu, Koil, Kovil, Mandir, Mandira, Prasaada, Raul, etc.

Mayamata, a treatise Vastusastra covering all the facets of gods' dwellings, gives 29 names as synonyms of mandir:

(1) Vimana, (2) Btiavana, (3) l-iarmya, (4) Soudha, (5) Diiama, (6) Niketan, (7) Prasada. (8) Sadana, (9) Sadma, (10) Geha, (11) Avasaka, (12) Grha, (13) Alaya. (14) Nilaya, (15) Vasa, (16) Aspada, (17) VasXu, (18) Vastika, (19) Ksetra, (20) Ayatana, (21) Vesma, (22) Mandira, (23) Dhisnyaka, (24) Pada, (25) Laya, (26) Ksaya, (27) Agara, (28) Udavasita and (29) Sthana.

Many of the names are synonyms for buildings or houses.

**Understanding a Mandir:** For a devotee, Mandir has many meanings. To some it represents universe to others it represents the sacred mountain and to some others something more.

---

5

Mandir as a Sacred Mountain: The mandir is built and perceived in the image of Mount Meru, the sacred mountain. Mount Meru represents ultimate knowledge and ascending it symbolizes attainment of self-realization. A mandir is conceived as Mount Meru because, above all, it is a spiritual institution. The Vimana or Shikhara of mandir is constructed to resemble a mountain. It is imagined as the sacred mountain because it facilitates the spiritual journey of man, from being an individual to realizing his oneness with the Supreme Consciousness. The mandir takes one on spiritual journey.

Mandir as Universe: "The Vastu Sastras identify the mandirs with the universe. Its substance and shape, says the Vastu section of Agnipurana, is Prakriti. The primordial nature and the central image enshrined therein is the Parama-purusha, the Supreme Spirit. The entire mandir is an organic whole consisting of the various limbs of that Purusha. Agnipurana says that the shikhara is the head, the dwara (door) the mouth, kalasa the hair, greeva the throat, shukanasa the nose, bhadras the arms, vedi the shoulders, stambha (pillar) the foot, etc. (Vastu Shastra and Temples Prof P Thirugnanasambandhan, Temple India, Vivekananda Kendra Patrika)

S. Satyamurti Ayyangar's words can be used to sum it up: The mandir constitutes our rich heritage. It will be no exaggeration to state that the tenacity of our Hindu culture rests upon the stable base of our mandirs, which have been the traditional centres fostering the growth of civilisation, in all its ramifications in art, literature, painting, sculpture, dance, drama, etc. (The Origin and Significance of Temples, S. Satyamurti Ayyangar, Temple in India, Vivekananda Kendra Patrika)

Mandir means many things at any given point of time, but in its order of importance it is a sacred structure first. In its most basic form, it is just an icon under a tree. An image is considered necessary for meditation, concrete or abstract, though concrete images are recommended for better facilitation. The barest and smallest of the mandirs fulfils the sacred goal of self-realization of a soul. This is kept utmost in mind while consecrating mandirs.

**Classification of Mandirs:** Classification of Mandirs can be done on different parameters. Some of them are:

I. Ownership

Atmartha or Svartha Shrine - A 'private shrine', meant for the individual devotee and for his family, anyone of the household can conduct puja.

Parartha Shrine - A public shrine meant for whole community. Only an authenticated priest is ordained to do puja.

II. Builder and Location

Scriptures like Padma Samhita and Sri Prashna Samhita make distinction among the mandirs based on the builder and the location of the mandirs.

Siddhayatana - These mandirs are built by great sages at serene spots, such as

<!-- page 13 -->

mountain-peaks, river-beds, where two or more rivers meet, at sea-shore and amidst the forests. These are great spots which are preferred by devotees for meditating on the supreme.

Assidhayatana - These mandirs are built by rajas and traders in busy places like the centre of a town. They are worshipped by the common people and fulfil a social need.

III. Building Material: Ancient mandirs made of wood are naturally lost. Mandirs in the cave and of stone were built from ancient times.

Pallava Emperors of Kanchi (590 CE) namely Mahendravarma Pallava built cave temples. The first such temple is the Mandahappattu temples for Brahma, Vishnu and Siva; the inscription says that Mahendra built this temple 'without the aid of brick, mortar, timber or metal'. He created such temples at Vallam, Dalavanur, Pallavaram, Mamandur, Mahendravadi, Siyamangalam, Tirukkalukkunram and Tiruchirappalli. He next started the monolithic temples at the place now known as Mahabalipuram, (Mamalla-puram). Rajasimha Pallava of Kanchi, (666-705 CE) commenced the new style of constructing temples of cut stones piled one over the other, a style which had come to stay to this day. The Kailasanatha temples of Kanchi, Iravatesvarar temples and Panaimalai temples are his creation. (Temples of Tamilnadu by M Arunachalam, Temple in India, Vivekananda Kendra Patrika)

Classifications based on building materials. There are three classes as under:

(a) Shuddha: It is constructed using only one material (stone, brick, timber and iron).

(b) Mishra: It is constructed using two types of materials.

(c) Samkirna: It is constructed using three or more materials like stone, brick, timber, etc.

The Ishanasiva Gurudeva Paddhati refers to three kinds of mandirs, the one made of stone or brick (sancita), brick or wood (asancita) and brick and wood (upasancita).

IV. Origin of Deity: Padma Purana and Paramesvara Samhita classify the Hindu mandirs into five types, based on the origin of the deity. The mandirs according to this classification are:

(a) Svayam Vyakta - Where the image of the deity is self-manifest and hence does not need consecration and other related rituals e.g., Amarnath mandir.

(b) Daivika - Where the iconic forms are believed to have been installed by divine beings, in places of exceeding purity e.g., Rameshwaram mandir, where lingam is installed by Shri Ram himself.

(c) Arsha - Shrines built by great sages in forest-retreats, by the power of their penance.

(d) Pauraana - The mandirs which were built during the age of the Puranas, and acclaimed in them. The mandir at Tirupati is a pauraanic type of mandirs as it is mentioned in the Puranas.

(e) Manusha - mandirs built by human beings - rajas, chieftains, devotees and consecrated by priests.

"While the first four kinds of places are holy by themselves, the last variety needs to be sanctified by special effort.

It is important to note that all the instructions about Vastu are for the fifth kind of mandir, the mandir built by human beings, the Manusha category.

(On What is a Hindu Temple by Pankaj Saxena, 10 June 2017, Indiafacts.org)

V. Postures of the Deity: These classifications are based on postures of the deity:

(a) Samcita (Samchita): Standing posture of the deity.

(b) Asamcita (Asamchita): Sitting posture of the deity.

(c) Apasancita (Apasnchita): Lying posture of the deity.

VI. Region and Architecture Styles: The most basic divisions based on regions and styles are:

(a) Nagara

(b) Vesara

(c) Dravida

VII. Scripture Based Classification: Different scriptures give different classifications for Mandirs. Some of them are:

(a) Brhatsamhita: Brhatsamhita classifies Mandir's into various types which are:

1. Meru, 2. Mandara, 3. Kailasa, 4. Vimanaccanda, 5. Nandana, 6. Samudra, 7. Padma, 8. Garuda, 9. Nandivardhana, 10. Kunjara or Hastiprsta, 11. Guharaja, 12. Vrsa, 13. Hamsa, 14. Ghata, 15. Sarvatobhadra 16. Simha, 17. Vrtta

(b) Manasara: Manasara classifies mandirs from single storey to twelve storeys. Only the number of types of mandirs pertaining to each storey is given below:

(1) Single storey - 8 types, (2) two storeys - 8 types, (3) three storeys - 8 types, (4) four storeys - 8 types, (5) five storeys - 8 types, (6) six storeys - 13 types, (7) seven storeys - 8 types, (8) eight storeys - 8 types, (9) nine storeys - 7 types, (10) ten storeys - 6 types, (11) eleven storeys - 6 types, (12) and twelve storeys - 10 types.

(c) Agnipurana: Agnipurana classifies mandirs into five main divisions depending on the basic shapes namely, quadrangular, rectangular, circular, oval and octagonal. Further sub classification takes the total number of classifications to 45 types.

(d) Garudapurana: Garudapurana gives the same number of classifications based on five basic shapes and gives nine sub divisions making total of 45 kinds of mandirs.

(e) Matsyapurana: Matsyapurana gives 20 divisions of the mandirs as:

(1) Meru, (2) Mandara, (3) Kailasa, (4) Vimanaccanda, (5) Nandivardhana, (6) Nandana, (7) Sarvatobhadra, (8) Vallabhiccandaka, (9) Vrisa, (10) Simha,

<!-- page 14 -->

(11) Gaja, (12) Kumbha, (13) Samudraka, (14) Padma, (15) Garuda, (16) Hama, (17) Vartula, (18) Caturasra, (19) Astasra, and (20) Sodasasra.

Most of the classifications given in Brhatsamhita, Garuda and Agni and Matsys purana have commonalties,

(f) Kamikagama: Kamikagama gives broad classifications of jati, ccanda, vikalpa and abhasa. Tantrasamuccaya (Silpabhaga) gives the classifications of alpa, jati, ccanda, vikalpa and abhasa prasadas depending on the width of prasadas and the number of storeys. Kasyapiya also contributes to the same school of thought and extends the number of storeys upto 16.

(g) Samaranganasutradhara: Samaranganasutradhara classifies mandirs as:

(1) Lalitaprasadas (25 types), sandhara prasadas (25 types), Nigudha prasadas (5 types) and mixed varieties (9 types)

(2) Based on the presiding deities 8 varieties such as Siva (8 types), Vishnu (8 types), Brahma (8 types), Surya (8 types), Candika (8 types), Vinayaka (8 types), Laksmi (8 types) and common to all deities (8 types). All varieties have superior, medium and inferior categories.

(h) Visnudharmotarapurana: Visnudharmotarapurana classifies mandirs into 100 types.

(i) Padmasamhita: Padmasamhita classifies mandirs into 49 varieties.

(j) Visveksenasamhita: Visveksenasamhita classifies mandirs into five types: Mandara, Nisadha, Nagara, Vesara and Dravida.

(k) Markandeyasamhita: Markandeyasamhita more or less agrees with the above but adds Indubhadra, Bhadraka, Trikuta and Vimala. The classifications given above are based on the plan, shapes, spaces, forms, decorations and styles. Though the varieties are large, there is unity in the basic concepts of shapes, spaces, forms, utility and decorations. (The Hindu Temples - a Glance, Chapter-3)

It is very clear that the world of 'Temple' and 'Mandir' is very different, and the word 'Temple' is no match for the word 'Mandir'. We Hindus should with immediate effect stop using the word "Temple" for "Mandir".

Temple is not Mandir. Mandir is not Temple.

**Economics or Arthashastra?**

*Though almost everyone has heard of GDP, few know it was invented as recently as the 1930s..before 1930s it practically did not exist. ....If GDP were a person, it would be indifferent, blind even, to morality. It measures production of whatever kind, good or bad. GDP likes pollution, particularly if you have to spend money clearing it up. It likes crime because it is fond of large police force and repairing broken windows. GDP likes Hurricane Katrina and is quite OK with wars. It likes to measure the build up to conflict*

*in guns, planes and warheads, then it likes to count all the effort in reconstructing shattered cities from the smouldering ruins. GDP is good at counting, but a pretty poor judge of quality.*

\- The Growth Delusion, 2018 by David Pillang, Bloomsbury

There is a vast difference between Economics and Arthashastra. In simple words, Economics is the social science that only analyses the production, distribution and consumption of goods and service and is not concerned with the ethical, moral, philosophical, and spiritual values.

International Monetary Fund's informal economy report talk about different aspects of GDP. Following is an excerpt: In the European Union, although all Member States are requested to include estimates of the output in prostitution in the national accounts, few are currently including estimates of the cross-border prostitution services in the external accounts. The later, when produced, are not separately published and the information available on the estimation methods is limited. In the context of the national accounts, the impact of the estimated value added of the prostitution industry in GDP ranges from less than 0.1% in Sweden (in 2006) and the Netherlands (in 2008) to 0.1% in Denmark (in 2004) and slightly over 0.2% in Italy (in 2011) and Luxembourg (in 2013). In the U.K., the Office for National Statistics estimates prostitution to have generated close to 0.3% of GDP. Contributions below 0.5% of GDP have been reported also for other countries, e.g., Spain, Germany and Portugal. (ECB: Estimation of Prostitution Services in Europe in the Context of the External Accounts, Informal Economy Reports, imf.org)

Prostitution is part of GDP. To some it may be shocking but it is not surprising. After all Western Economy grew from 'Slave Economy' to 'Mercantile Economy' to 'Market Economy'. In 1662 Virginia (USA) passed law referring to Negroes as slaves. Fogel & Engerman found that slavery was highly profitable and 35% more efficient than northern family farming.

Marvin Brown wrote: 'The reality of commerce when Adam smith was composing "The Wealth of Nations" was something else. The centre of this trade was not the town square, but the Atlantic Ocean, which was used for the trafficking of millions of captive Africans. Robin Blackburn estimates that of the 21 million Africans enslaved between 1700 and 1850, nine million slaves were delivered to the America, slavery was an economic institution. (Marvin Brown, "Free enterprise and the economics of slavery", real-world economics review, issue no. 52, 7 March 2010, pp. 28-39)

One Mississippi planter had pointed out "If the price of the cotton was high enough, it would make economic sense to kill up and wear out one negro to buy another". (False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management And Why Their Ideas Are Bad For Business Today (2003) by James Hoopes, Perseus Publishing.)

When British, Portuguese, French, Dutch landed in Bharat, to their shock they found

Arthashastra is what west needs. Arthashastra made Bharat prosperous. Arthashastra has been around long before economy or economics came into existence. Arthashastra is comprehensive, all-encompassing. It was perfected by Acharya Chanakya and implemented in the Mauryan empire. It is time tested.

Acharya Chanakya pointed out: "Arth has a much wider significance than merely 'wealth'. The material wellbeing of individual is a part of it. … Artha is an all-embracing word with a variety of meanings... it is used in the sense of material well-being; livelihood; economically productive activity, particularly in agriculture, cattle rearing and trade; and, in general, wealth as in the 'Wealth of Nations'. The state or government has a crucial role to play in maintaining the material well-being of the nation and its people. Therefore, an important part of Arthashastras is 'the science of economics', including starting productive enterprises, taxation, revenue collection, budget and accounts. […] an integral part of Arthashastra is dandaniti, the enforcement of laws by a voluminous and comprehensive set of fines and punishments." When work is done for a community it becomes a form of prayer, non-exploitative

For better appreciation let us recognise the difference between Economics and Arthashastra through a small case study.

**Case Study - I: Difference between Industrial Economics and Mandir based Arthashastra**

To grasp the difference between Industrial Economics and Mandir based Arthashastra, let us take the example of Detroit. Detroit being the heart of the American automotive industry, got the name "Motor City." The state's automotive industry provided the model for mass production those other industries later adopted. Henry Ford pioneered the use of the assembly line in manufacturing automobiles in Detroit. But Census data of USA of 2011 said Detroit is dying. ... From 2000 to 2010, Detroit lost a quarter of its population. In 2010, it was the 18th largest U.S. city. In 2019, it was 24th.

It became cheaper to manufacture car in various Asian countries and the manufacturing shifted from Detroit. There was nothing inherent in the vehicles manufactured at Detroit which could keep the consumers attached to it.

Other cities which were big losers of population are: Cleveland-17%, Cincinnati-10.4%, Pittsburgh-8.6%, Toledo- 8.4%. These cities were once known as cities of New Economy, today collectively they are known as Rust Belt. Atlantic City of United States is renowned resort city for gambling, shopping and fine dining. The city also served as the inspiration for the board game Monopoly. Today it is a dying city. In 1930, its population was 66,198, and as per 2010 survey it is 39,558. It is 9th in the list of Americas 10 dying cities. It is dying because all over the world more and more cities are offering new format of gambling, shopping, fine dining and lot more.

Compared to this, some of the oldest cities in the world with continuous habitation are Varanasi, Ujjain, Madurai, Pushkar etc. None are known for their industry but all of them known for their Mandirs. Arthavyavastha centred around Mandirs have sustained cities for thousands of years.

It is not surprising that as per Angus Maddison's study of the world economy, in the year One CE, Bharat's share of World GDP was 32.9 percent. (The World Economy Volume 1: A Millennial Perspective Volume 2: Historical Statistics, 2006 Angus Maddison, Development Centre of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development)

Industrial Economics has a finite time period while Mandir based Arthashastra is eternal. Industrial Economics is about profitability of an individual or a corporate. It is not about well-being of citizens or society. While in case of mandir based arthavyavastha, it is about well-being of its devotees, vendors or customers i.e., everyone in the value chain.

It is important that we Hindus get the name of abode of our Bhagwan correct, distinguish the difference between Arthashastra and Economics. Lot of things will fall

<!-- page 16 -->

in place for we Hindus if we can get the nomenclature right and understand the importance of terms.

## 2. Mandir Based Arthavyavastha

*It is the Deity around whom the entire fabric of Nathdwara's religion and economy rotates. The temple provides work to as many as 1000 families supporting at least 5000 souls. The rest of the population subsists on industries which are indirectly associated either with various functions, feasts and festivals of the temple or fulfil the needs of the pilgrims. Thus, the origin, evolution and entire prosperity of the town can be traced, in part, to the shifting of the idol to Nathdwara and in part to the pilgrims who visit the shrine.*

\- Culture of a Sacred Town, 1976 by R Jindel, Popular Prakashan

### Mandir's Revenue vs Mandir based Arthavyavastha

Money offered by devotees at the mandir and revenue earned by mandirs due to landed property is not "mandir based arthavyavastha" (Temple Economics), but just 'Mandir's revenue' (Temple Revenue). Mandir's revenue is a 'subset' of mandir based arthavyavastha (Image-1). It is important to have clarity on this because often one sees arguments being made for and against mandirs using phrases like 'Temple Economy' without understanding 'Mandir based Arthavyavastha'.

*[Figure: Diagram showing Mandir based Arthavyavastha (Temple Economics) as outer circle and Mandir Revenue (Temple Revenue) as inner circle. (Image-1)]*

### Mandir based Arthavyavastha

Temple Economy is a new concept. Mandir based arthavyavastha is as old as mandir. The money was generated and circulated in the society because of mandir, making it prosperous and over time wealthy. The right word is not wealthy but vaibhavshali. Vaibhav is beyond wealth. It encompasses richness with power, intelligence, ethics, and morality. One of the earliest detailed account of mandir-based arthavyavastha written in English by a Bhartiya, that I could find is the book "The Economy of a South Indian Temple" written in 1946 (Anamalai University) by V G Ramakrishna Aiyer. He writes:

"Though the construction' of temples and the provision for worship therein by grants of lands seem to be common, there is a vast amount of epigraphical evidence to show that temple charities were not exclusively meant for ceremonials in the temple but also for scientific' (sastraic) and religious (Vedic) education. The South Indian temples served the purposes of educational institutions. Provisions were

<!-- page 17 -->

made for the recitation in temples of hymns from the Devaram and other religious poems and for the reading and expounding works of great merit. Adhyayana (i.e., the chanting of the Vedas) was one of the many objects for which grants were made. A large number of records register grants made for the singing of the Tiruppadiyam and the Tiruvaymoli hymns. One inscription records the provision made for the rending' of the Epics like the Mahabhrata and the Ramayana and the Puranas. One of the Tiruvorriyur inscriptions states that as many as 60 velis were given for the maintenance of a mandapa built in the temple, for the upkeep of the teachers and pupils who studied grammar in that hall, and, for the worship of the god. Sivadharman and Siddhanta were also taught. In a stone inscription from the Venkatesa Perumal temple at Tirumukkudal near Conjeevaram it is stated that besides a hospital, the temple maintained a hostel and college. An epigraph' of the time of Rajendara Chola I at Ennayiram (South Arcot District) gives many interesting details to show that temples of South India served the purpose of educational institutions. This inscription is of great importance for it shows clearly that in ancient temples not only was the regular conducting of worship maintained, but also the study of the Vedas, philosophy, grammar and other sciences, and in a few cases, provision was made for a few persons versed in the Vedas. A few of the inscriptions provide grants for the recitation, of the Mahabharat and one of them provides for the recitation of the Bharata in a mandapa of the temple at Sendalai. A similar endowment occurs in the Kuram plates. Provision' seems to have been made now and then for the maintenance of a feeding house e.g., provision for feeding 50 students of Sastras.

There are several epigraphs to show the encouragement given to theatres and dances. In the larger South Indian temples, there was invariably a spacious Ranga Mandapa. Dancing was practised here and on special occasions dances were staged. The provisions for the amusement of visitors thronging from distant places to witness festivals in temples are occasionally met within inscriptions. An interesting epigraph records a gift of land to a professional actor for staging themes from Sanskrit Puranas. Another epigraph records the provision made for the maintenance of a theatre called Nanavida-natasalai while two other records register a gift of land for the performance of a dance called Sakki-kuttu and Sandi-kuttn respectively. The encouragement of music received attention, as for instance, a grant was made Vinaikkami for providing; music on the Vinai in the 'presence of the god on occasions of worship. An inscription in the Tmdisvara temple (Tmdivanam) dated in the 10th year (994 + 11 of the great Chola King Rajaraja I register's a grant of land for maintenance of a musician who was to play on the lute (Vinai).

There are a few instances of a purely literary matter engraved on stone, e.g., music inscription at Kudimiymalai, the Bharatanatyam verses at Chidambaram, the Devaram inscription at Tiruvidavayil.

The South Indian temple was thus the seat of free culture. The temples not only served a social and religious purpose but also were of educational value. The reading of the epics and the recitation of the hymns enabled the people to faithfully follow their religion and enrich their minds. Some of the great classical works in Tamil are said to have been composed in temples.

Closely connected with the temples, there were many Vaishnava and Saiva mathams which were both teaching institutions and their educative influence was very great, especially in the Vedas and Sastras and the Puranas. The 'mathams', were important religious institutions They were encouraged by the State and possessed a vast amount of wealth'- There was a religious head for each 'matham' who was highly respected. Generally, every matham stood for the propagation of a particular school or religion and encouraged teaching and the spreading of knowledge in religious lore. Many pious gifts were made to these institutions by the rulers as well as the people and these 'mathams' figured as important adjuncts of the temples for the preservation of traditional culture.

A sketch of the main features of the South Indian temple will be incomplete without a reference to their architecture, sculpture and painting. The temple architecture reflects the spiritual ideals of the people. The South Indian temples are standing monuments of Dravidian architecture. The temple craftsman kept alive the traditions of building and metal working embodied in the Silpasastras by which all great public works were regulated. Speaking of the Dravidian style of architecture Professor Jouveau Dubreud observes: The Pallava period (600 - 850) is that of sculptured rocks, the early Chola period (850 - 1100) that of grand Vimanas, the later Chola period (1350 - 1600) that of the most beautiful Gopuras, the Vijayanagar period (1350 - 1600) that of Mandapas (pillared halls) and the modern period after 1600 that of corridors".

In brief the great temples of South India were public 'institutions' representing the collective energy of the state rather than monuments for the king's personal glorification. They had civic as well as religious uses; they fulfilled the purposes of a town-hall, college and technical school. The people met in the temple porches to elect representatives for local bodies, to listen to sacred music, recitations or plays. The schools attached to the temple were the repositories of the philosophical lore which were the mainspring of religious life.

The records of the religious movements in which the South Indian rulers took an active part have been carefully preserved in both Sanskrit and vernacular literatures, and in Sankaracharya's and Ramanuja's famous commentaries, in the hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar and in the Tamil puranas. "Many temples built by royal command are memorials of them. Images of the 'Saints and Alwars', who composed hymns in praise of Siva and Visnu, were set up in temple precincts

<!-- page 18 -->

16

and the temple structures breathing the spirit of bhakti prove the 'extraordinary richness of the artistic resources which the rulers commanded. But the temples they built tell nothing of their lives except brief summaries of conquests which made so little impression on the popular memory that whole dynasties, were forgotten, although their temples are still in daily use."

To sum it up, mandirs were place of science, technology, philosophy, art (craft, music, dance, theatre) and education. Students were provided end to end support, that is from grant to hostel facility. Professional artists were supported through grants. Community decisions were taken in the mandir. Mathams were integral part of mandir in all these initiatives. Apart from religious function, mandirs were responsible for social and civic duties. Undoubtedly the arthavyavastha of the city revolved around the mandirs. The most important part, mandirs represented the state and not the raja.

Some Islamist invaders kept one or two mandirs functioning in their occupied area so that they can make money out of them. Christian invaders were also aware of this. Invading British understood the vitality of Mandir based arthavyavastha and they used it to revive settlements. "In 1783, as soon as the English took over the direct administration of the Jaghir, the 'Superintendent' Richard Dighton was asked by the Jaghir Committee to conduct an inquiry and report on the best way to re-establish the mandirs which are in a ruined condition. Recreating the mandirs, it was felt would contribute greatly towards restoring the country to its former flourishing state, by drawing together its dispersed inhabitants." (The View From Below, 2004 by Kanakalatha Mukund, Orient Blackswan).

British started with the use of mandir treasuries to rejuvenate ruined cities and then went on to squeeze every penny from the mandir and its devotees. Nothing has changed for mandirs even after transfer of power in 1947. But before that let us look at two case studies based on two mandirs from two different parts of Bharat but both standing and supporting the devotees in their hour of need.

**Case Study - I: Arthavyavastha based on Palani Mandir**

Palani mandir is one of the six abodes of Bhagwan Murugan and considered the most prominent of the abodes of Murugan. 'After Tirupati temple, Palani temple gets and earns the highest revenue. Revenue of the temple was Rs. 114.49 crores in 2012, and Rs. 111.12 crores in 2011. Temple entry ticket collection alone rose to Rs 25 crore, 2 per cent up from previous year. While leasing the land owned by the Palani temple alone earned Rs. 17 lakh, hiring out the buildings fetched an amount of Rs. 57 lakh (The Hindu, 3 August 2012). What is significant is that the Palani mandir did not rest on laurels of its revenue but used it efficiently and turned into the nucleus of the arthavyavastha of the city.

C. Arul Jothi has documented in detail, the all-around economic or aarthic activities undertaken by the Palani mandir:

17

Palani temple has a total of 33 Hundis including three "Navathanya Hundies" (The Devasthanam has installed a "Navathanya Hundi" to enable agriculturists to give their produce as offerings). The Hundi, or the cash box is the backbone of the economy of the temple. Every devotee contributes what they can afford and, it may be currency, replica parts of the body like eye or ear in gold or silver to thank god for getting back vision or power of hearing. The officers of the temple open the hundi in the presence of the trustees periodically and the contents are scrutinized, categorized, counted, weighed, tabulated and properly accounted. The total receipts are announced time to time and published in the reports.

Because of the temple, the town was constituted into a municipality on 1st April 1886 with a population of 13,315. Palani was upgraded as Grade II municipality in November 1949. Palani was further upgraded as grade I municipality in April 1982. Now it is functioning as selection grade municipality since from 01.12.1988. The total area of the town is 6.63 sqkm with a population of 70,467 as per 2011 census.

The study reveals the existence of 287 small shops selling various articles on the four streets of the Advivaram. 78 taxis, 160 autorickshaws and 21 jutkas (horse driven carriage) were operating there apart from the local town buses. There are 329 barbers offering services for tonsure ceremony. Various cottage industries of this place produce products which are used in the temple.

Socio-Economic Activities of the Palani Temple:

The first category of the welfare activities deals with the educational institutions:

1. Oriental college was established in 1960 with the object of spreading the significance of religion, culture and spiritualism. Students of this college are taught subjects like Sanskrit, Devaram and vocal music along with their conventional subjects.

2. Arts college for boys in 1963, a separate college for girls was started in 1970.

3. A polytechnic for women was established in 1981 followed by a Polytechnic for men in 1982.

4. To protect and promote the classical art like Naadasvaram and Thavil Palani, Devasthanam has established the Naadasvaram College in 1957 with a four-year course under the Gurukula method, the only institution of its kind in south of India. **Without this Bharat may have lost Naadasvaram, as an instrument.** The total strength of the students was 40 in Naadasvaram section and 29 in Thavil. All the students of this college are provided free education with free boarding and lodging, clothing and medical facilities.

5. To improve the depth in Tamil literature a separate college for women called Sentamil College was established in 1970. The 'Pulavar' and a Diploma certificate is given to qualifying students.

<!-- page 19 -->

6. The Veda Agama School is functioning from 1959, covers the subjects related to the temple pooja service, performance of Tamil Archana, Conduct of Kumbhabhishekama and other festivals. A five-year intensive training is given to the students with the provisions of food, dress, accommodation and medical aid, free of charge. At the end of the fifth year the student is awarded with the title called "Agamamani". The present strength is 25 and so far, 71 persons have been issued diplomas.

7. There is Palani Andavar Matriculation School

8. A School for the deaf at primary level with the necessary equipment's was established in 1972. All the 25 students of this school are provided with free boarding and lodging and medical aid.

9. Devasthanam is maintaining Andavar Library consisting of 5500 books with 15 monthly magazines, 16 weeklies and 11 daily newspapers since 1985.

The second category of the welfare activities deals with the health, sanitation:

1. The Devasthanam spends a considerable amount jointly with the Palani Municipality to eradicate Pollution and contagious disease.

2. The Devasthanam is running a Siddha dispensary since 1964, imparting free treatment to all patients.

3. An Allopathic hospital is also being maintained since 1972.

The third category of the welfare activities deals with the social responsibility:

1. It provides all facilities for the 183 orphaned boys including their educational expenditure. This asylum also accommodates aged people. The inmates are provided with all the necessities of life free of cost.

2. Under the mid-day meals scheme launched in 1958, nearly 700 to 800 poor school children were given free lunch every year. But after the introduction of the 'Chief Minister's Mid-Meal Scheme' this was given up.

3. The creche for pre-school children level benefiting employed poor parents has been established in 1972. These children are given milk, lunch, biscuits and medical aid free of charge.

The fourth category of the welfare activities deals with helping other temples in and outside Bharat:

For the improvement of other religious institution. For this it has created a fund called "The Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Common Good Fund" under the provision of HR and CE Act XIX of 1951 section 97(1). As per this provision Palani Devastanam has deposited Rs 100 Lacs in fixed account with an approved bank and has regularly contributed to other temples from the interest received from the above sum. The temple in Adi Sankara Shrine at Prayag,

Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh and The Thirukedeesvaram Siva temple in Sri Lanka have been helped financially.

The fifth category of the welfare activities deals with the weaker section of the society:

1. Since 1981, temple also conducts mass marriages and takes care of all expenses. Between 1981 and 1982 forty-four such marriages have been conducted by this institution.

2. Temple also maintains a marriage hall.

The sixth category of the welfare activities deals with building a cohesive society:

Community feast, another social function clubbed with poojas, a type of get together of all categories of people irrespective of caste and status, has been conducted since 1981.

During his visit to Palani mandir C Anna Rao the Executive Officer of Tirupati Tirumala Devasthanam has noted, "The temple is being improved from time to time with institutions like college of oriental culture and Nathaswaram Section attached to the Temple. As a matter of fact, we at Tirupati have established these institutions taking Palani temple as an example." Here spiritualism and materialism have been inseparably intermingled with each other, contrary to the common statement that where spiritualism ends, materialism begins and vice versa.

(Pilgrimage Tourism and Changing Local Livelihood A Study of Temple Town of Palani, Tamil Nadu; Thesis submitted to The Gandhigram Rural Institute, 2012 by C. Arul Jothi)

A city with a population of just 70,467 as per 2011 census has 392 barbers. Undoubtedly, it is the mandir which is providing livelihood to so many barbers through its devotees who come here and offer their hair. The mandir provide mid-day meals to the students in its schools before any government started it. It had a creche in 1972. Not only it maintained hospital but also had a school for deaf students in 1972. Mandir preserved vocal music as well as conducted mass marriages. Mandir looked after cleaning the city and ran school for blind. And yes, it supported mandirs at far off places. No wonder the city was converted into a municipality in 1886 because of mandir. What better live example of a city whose arthavyavastha is based on mandir.

Last but not the least, the study noted that significance is not given to welfare activities especially during the latter years of the study period. Does it mean, after coming under the secular government, the welfare activities declined?

## **Case Study -II: Arthavyavastha based on Jwalamukhi Mandir**

The Kangra mandir cluster in Himachal Pradesh has a large number of mandirs such as Ashapuri mandir, Ambika Devi, Vajreshvari mandir, Chamunda Devi mandir, Kaleshvara mandir, Thardvara mandir, Baijnatha mandir, Indravara mandir, Jwalamukhi mandir etc. The mandir of the Jwalamukhi is located in the Kangra district. The Hindi word 'Jwalamukhi' means 'Volcano' in English. Hindu genealogy registers

<!-- page 20 -->

are kept here like that of those in Haridwar.

Jwalamukhi is one of the holy places where the tongue of Sati fell and Shakti appears in the form of flames. Here Devi appears in the form of nine different flames. The main flame is in the front, namely Mahaakali. Like any other mandir, even Jwalamukhi mandir contributes to the welfare activity, it acted as money lander to the devotees:

Some letters written to the pradhan (president) of the temple Shri Jwalamukhi for lending money have been found. This request was not only by the priestly class but even the local people of other castes requested to the Prabandhkarini committee, Shri Jwalamukhi, to lend them a certain amount.

A letter shows that a request was made to the Prabandhkarini committee; to lend him Rs 200 for the treatment of his daughter by a fellow named Madan Lal whose profession and caste are not known and his request was taken into consideration.

Pujari Braj Kishore made a request for Rs 200 for the delivery of his wife, which was granted money was also borrowed for the treatment of their daughter.

Pujari Kala Dutt Sharma requested for Rs 100 for the treatment of his son-in-law. Pujari Shiv Lal also requested for Rs 100 as his wife was not keeping well.

A request was made for the treatment to be taken outside as the treatment could be had only in a bigger hospital since the cure was not possible locally. Accordingly, a request was made by Baladath Sharma, who was suffering from stomach ache and wanted to get himself treated either in Jalandhar or Hoshiarpur.

In another letter, Hari Chand Sharma, who also wanted to get himself treated out of Jwalamukhi, requested for loan of Rs. 200. Bander Sharma of Kangra also requested for Rs 200 for his treatment.

The purpose of demand for money varied from person to person as per their requirements. There is an instance where a certain amount of money was borrowed for their daughter's marriage also. Madanlal (it is not clear whether it is same person who requested for help for his daughter's treatment) requested the committee to lend him Rs. 1000 to bear the expenses of his sister's marriage. His economic condition was in bad shape but he would return the amount after navratras. Whatever he would earn, during navratras, he would hand over to the committee. The evidence also comes across that when certain amount was demanded, people also assured the committee of its return when they would earn during the navratras.

In another record, Kamal Prasad Sharma made a request for Rs. 200 to attend his nephew's marriage and his request was taken into consideration and Rs. 200 was granted to him.

Pujari Rajnikant Sharma of Jwalamukhi requested for a loan of Rs. 400 as he had to pay back the money which he had borrowed to put up with the expenses of his sister's marriage. It is not mentioned as to how he would return the money.

Shankri Devi also requested the president of the Prabandhkarini committee for a Rs. 1500 loan to meet the expenses of her son's marriage.

In another instance, it is found that money was also borrowed to attend the marriage of their relatives. Prakash Chand Sharma had to attend the marriage of one of his relatives and he requested for a loan of Rs. 100.

At times, it is found that the temple committee lent not only money but commodities also. A person named Nathu Ram requested the committee to lend him something on the occasion of his daughter's marriage, as he was a poor man and it was difficult for him to bear all the expenses of the marriage. So, the temple committee decided to lend him Rs. 20 and 1 maund of Rice. It was charity on the part of the temple as Nathu Ram did not mention how he would return the money, nor there is any evidence that he was asked to sign any paper.

Most of the records do not reveal how the money would be returned; but the people returned money on time.

The provision for lending and taking money remained there till the early 60's. There is no evidence to suggest money was borrowed from the temple after 1965.

(Jawalamukhi Temple as a Lender by Pallavi Mishra, Vol 2 Issue 9, September, 2014, The International Journal Of Science & Technoledge.)

It is definite that in the past, the temple stood by people in their hour of need. The temple met the need of the day by assuming the role of a money lender and financed people in their various endeavours

The mandir is multifaceted as it works not only as an employer, consumer or lender. In the past, the mandir worked as an assembly point where people gathered to resolve their disputes or to celebrate marriage. At the Jwalamukhi mandir, the marriages are performed. The mandir was a place for coronation and other important functions also.

The mandir also served as a service centre. An Ayurvedic Dispensary is maintained by the Jwalamukhi mandir.

The mandirs continued to be the most important centre of philanthropic activities. They maintained choultries. Earlier, in the Jwalamukhi mandir, the choultries were erected by the maharaja of Patiala. Subsequently, Narendra Singh, maintained them till it was funded by maharaja Patiala, though now it is standing on its last legs, but many other choultries have been opened by the traders. Earlier, it was the custom of providing alms to beggars from the mandir fund. The Jwalamukhi mandir has exercised a benevolent and profound influence on the life of the people and has played pivotal roles in the social order.

Mandir provided financial help to its devotees cutting across caste. It maintained a dispensary plus provided money for medical treatment to marriage. It is not a very rich mandir but it remains a centre of arthavyavastha in its own way.

<!-- page 21 -->

Mandirs in all parts of Bharat took care of the society's arthavyavastha. Mandirs were centres of education, music, song, dance, literature etc. Mandir was consumer, employer and lender too. Mandir belonged to the devotee. At the time of distress be it emotional, philosophical, financial or any other need, the devotee was free to approach the Bhagwan. Mandirs took care of social responsibility through hostel or schools for blind. They stood for other mandirs when there was need. There was no differentiation based on region or sect. Such was mandir based arthavyavastha, not surprising that Bharat had a happy society and it was a prosperous nation.

## 3. Why Mandir based Arthavyavastha?

*I asked the guide at Trichinopoly how the people of India had found, three or four hundred years ago, the money to build the vast temples there and at Madura and Tanjore. He answered that the rajahs had been able to build these edifices despite the fact that they had taxed the people much less severely than the English were doing.*

\- The Case For India, 1930 by Will Durant, Strand Book Stall

In January, 1750, Marthanda Varma "donated" his rajya to Sri Padmanaabha (Vishnu) and thereafter ruled as the deity's "vice-regent" (Sri Padmanaabha Dasa). This was followed by the Marthanda Varma's successor. Giving away rajya to Bhagwan by Raja Marthanda Varma and ruling on his behalf by him and his successors was not the first instance rather most probably it was the last instance in Bharat.

The Pandya and later day Nayak Rajas ruled as representatives of Devi Meenakshi. Every year the Raja used to come to the mandir and take the sceptre from the Devi in a ceremony and return it the next day.

Bappa Rawal a firm devotee of Eklingji placed his entire rajya at the feet of the deity. He proclaimed Eklingji as its ruler and regarded himself as the dewan or agent of the deity, ruling the rajya on behalf of the deity.

Raja Anangahhimadeva III called himself a Ravuta or a deputy of Purushottama at Puri and dedicated his rajya to the Bhagwan. Anangahhimadeva III ruled from 1211-1238. This tradition was maintained in Odisha after that by all the subsequent Rajas, irrespective of the dynasties.

**Dharm and Religion**

We Hindus must comprehend the difference between the words 'Dharm' and 'Religion'. The term "dharm" has no equivalence in any other language. Rajiv Malhotra in his article "Dharma Is Not The Same As Religion", (26 September 2011, Huffpost.com) writes:

"Dharma has the Sanskrit root dhri, which means "that which upholds" or "that without which nothing can stand" or "that which maintains the stability and harmony of the universe." Dharma encompasses the natural, innate behaviour of things, duty, law, ethics, virtue, etc. Every entity in the cosmos has its particular dharma - from the electron, which has the dharma to move in a certain manner, to the clouds, galaxies, plants, insects, and of course, man. Man's understanding of the dharma of inanimate things is what we now call physics."

Maria Wirth, in her article 'It is High Time that Hindus Woke Up' (22 December 2015, indiafacts.org) makes this distinction clearer. She compares two of the biggest religions in the world with Dharm, (Table-1):

We Hindus need to stop using 'Dharm' and 'Religion' interchangeably. Words play a very important role in influencing the mind; more so when it comes to civilisational issues.

### Dharmic Framework of Arth

Our ancestors realised that wealth alone can be dangerous. They cautioned the society in different ways. Symbolism and word play were one of important ways. Some of the examples of the same are:

Symbolism: Kubera is the guardian of treasures. His pet mongoose spits out precious gems. Unlike other gods who travel on animals and birds, he travels on the backs of human beings. He is not represented as handsome person. Thus, though wealth is crucial, this symbolism tells us that by itself, wealth is not beautiful and it can enslave a human being.

Words: Laabh i.e., profit is not acceptable in isolation. It has to be auspicious i.e., Shubh-Laabh. Profit which is earned by causing pain to others is not welcome. It has to be earned without causing discomfort to others.

Blackmail: One must note that there is no word in any Bhartiya language for the word 'Blackmail', because many of these concepts did not exist in Bharat. These initiatives paid dividends. The honesty of Hindu businessmen is documented in the literature too. Pattinappalai, one of the ten poems of the Pattuppattu said of the merchants of Puhar:

*The merchants of Puhar are as straight forward as the crosspiece of a yoke. They always speak the truth and are fair minded, and fear ignominy. They value their goods and the goods of others by the same standard; they neither take too high a price for their goods, nor do they short-change on what they sell. They openly state their profits on the various goods they handle. Such merchants lined in Puhar for many years.* (The World of the Tamil Merchant: Pioneers of International Trade, 2015 by Kanakalatha Mukund, Portfolio Penguin)

Today one may not see high level of ethical practices by some Hindu businessman, because business just like society at large got influenced by the practices of invaders. Following two paragraphs validate it.

*The Nazar system was a defining feature of Islamic regimes in India. In practice, it normalised political and official corruption at all levels beginning with the monarch himself, and was responsible for disfiguring the ancient Sanatana ideals of Dharma and Karma.* (The Islamic System of Nazar as a Source of Corruption, Sandeep Balakrishna, 1 November 2021, dharmadispatch.in)

*'It is a sad truth', the letter went on, 'that in all parts of India where the European generally come the natives soon learn to flatter, cheat, and wreck their malice whereas in the inland counties where few Europeans ever are, they are generally harmless and innocent and not inclined to mischief. The difference must be from the ill examples of those who call themselves Christians'.* - Dispatch Book, 10 January 1711, Vol 97, para 83, pp 1790 - 80

(The Trading World of Asia And The English East India Company: 1660-1760, 2006 by K.N. Chaudhuri, Cambridge University Press)

The honesty in business in Bharat was there from the earliest of time, because artha was prequalified by Dharm. Through this a boundary line was drawn on what one can do and cannot do to make money.

Ramayan (9-30, 31, Aranya Kanda) says:

"Wealth comes out of Dharma; Happiness comes out of Dharma.

Everything is obtainable from Dharma; Dharma is the essence of this universe"

Manibis besides being Bhagwan's residence, representation of a human, and many more things are also physical manifestation of 'Dharm'. Mandirs are also called "Dharmasthala or Dharmakshetra".

### Integration of Dharm and Arth

Our scriptures have expounded about the integration of Dharm and Arth. Manusmriti beautifully describes how Dharm and Arth are connected.

To achieve welfare and happiness some declare Dharma and Artha are good. Others declare that Artha and Kaama are better. Still others declare that Dharma is the best. There are also persons who declare Artha alone secures happiness. But the correct view is that the aggregate of Dharma, Artha and Kaama (Trivarga) secures welfare and happiness. However, the desire (kaama) and material wealth (Artha) must be rejected if contrary to Dharma

Justice M Rama Jois elaborated the integration in terms of Trivarga:

The propounders of Dharma did appreciate that the fulfilment of desires of human being was an essential aspect of life, but they were of the opinion that unless the desires were regulated by Dharma, undesirable results were bound to follow. Therefore, all the propounders of Dharma were unanimous that for the existence of an orderly society, peace and happiness of all, the desires (kaama) for material enjoyment and pleasures (artha) should always conform to Dharma (Law) and never be inconsistent with it. As a result, the doctrine of Trivarga i.e., Dharma, Artha, Kaama was laid down. The injunction to every individual flowing from the doctrine of Trivarga was that the desire (Kaama) and material wealth (Artha) must be rejected if it is contrary to Dharma.

Before proceeding further, it is important to note that Kaama is not Lust. To quote Rajiv Malhotra et al:

The word kama which is often translated as 'lust' or 'sex'. Lust is defined as a strong emotion or feeling that manifests in the form of an intense yearning for sex, expensive objects, power, even food; lust is a powerful psychological force and produces an overwhelming desire for its object. Kaama derives from the Sanskrit root kama which primarily means 'desire'. The dharmic point of view considers kama as one of the four purusharthas-s or goals of human life along with dharma, artha and moksha. The original and primary kama of every sentient being is happiness which can be fulfilled through various means; thus kama is a more fundamental and broader concept and not simply lust. The pursuit of kama is the result of the disconnect between a jivatma and the anand of the Brahman (Sachidananda), due to the jiva identifying itself only with material reality. It is thus pursuit which manifests in yearning for various objects, furthered by misidentifying oneself with physical, emotional and mental entities. Hinduism recognizes this entanglement and provides a structure to legitimately pursue kama without letting it degenerate into mere lust. According to Hindu dharma, kama should not be satisfied in a way that becomes self-perpetuating and an obstacle to dharma or artha. The ancient Indian treatise of Kaamasutra written by Vatsyaayana says that indulgence in kama, which means sexual enjoyment in this treatise, should not be at the expense of dharma and artha. Similarly, in the Arthashastra, written by Kautilya, it is said that a person should not make money in a way that goes against the dharma. Thus, the word kama used in the shastra-s denotes a concept which is regulated by the scriptural injunctions and is not an unbridled pursuit like lust (Sanskrit Non-Translatables, 2020 by Rajiv Malhotra and Satyanarayana Dasa Babaji, Amaryllis)

Most Hindu concepts have been misunderstood by we Hindus because we read them in English. The translations in English are not only defective (Sanskrit words cannot be translated) but they are done from the western translator's construct, which is mostly biased against we Hindus.

Coming back to 'Dharm' and 'Arth', business law in medieval and early modern Bharat was developed under the voluminous and multifaceted texts called the Dharmashastras. Donald R Davis Jr. writes 'These texts lay down rules for merchants, guilds, families, and other individuals in terms of the complex religious, commercial, legal and moral ideal of dharma. Most Dharmashastra contain a separate section on the eighteen titles of substantive law. Among these titles of law, eight deal directly with business-related matters. These eight are

1. Non-payment of debts
2. Deposits
3. Sale without Ownership
4. Partnerships
5. Non-payment of Wages
6. Breach of Sale or Purchase
7. Violations of Business Standards
8. Disputes between Employer & Employees

The rules of Artha have been set through Dharmashastra and the Artha revolved around the Mandir i.e., loosely the economics always revolved around the temple. 'It is true that many area covered by the Arthashastra are also included in the Dharmashastras. There is, however, a crucial difference between the two. The Dharmashastras address themselves to the individual, teaching him his dharma, and regard deviations from it as sins to be expiated by ritual. The Arthashastras are addressed to rulers and regard transgressions of law as crimes to be punished by the state.

Artha follows dharm. As used in Arthashastras generally and by Kautilya, the last and greatest master of the science, artha has a much wider significance than merely 'wealth'. The material well-being of individuals is a part of it. As Kautilya says in the concluding section of his book: 'The source of the livelihood of men is wealth'. He then draws the corollary that the wealth of a nation is both the territory of the state and its inhabitants who may follow a variety of occupations. The state or government has a crucial role to play in maintaining the material well-being of the nation and its people. Therefore, an important part of Arthashastras is 'the science of economics', including starting a productive enterprises, taxation, revenue collection, budget and accounts.

Artha is an all-embracing word with a variety of meanings. It is used in the sense of material well-being, livelihood, economically productive activity, particularly in

---

29

agriculture, cattle rearing and trade; and, in general, wealth as in the 'Wealth of Nations'. Arthashastra is, thus, 'the science of politics'. It is the art of government in its widest sense. The subjects covered include: administration; law, order and justice, taxation, revenue and expenditure, foreign policy, defence and war. Its three objectives follow one from the other: promotion of the welfare of the subjects leads to acquisition of wealth which, in turn, makes it possible to enlarge the territory by conquest." (The Arthashastra Edited, Rearranged & Translated from the Sanskrit, 1992 by L.N. Rangarajan, Penguin Classics)

A very popular myth about Hindus is that they are otherworldly and not interested in material world. Though right from Ramayan to Mahabharat there is detailed discussion on importance of material life. Acharya Chanakya explicitly mentioned about connect between Dharm and Arth. He said that the basis of Dharm is Arth. He elaborated the same in his sutra, famously knows as Chanakya Sutra (Table-4). The sutra clearly establishes the functioning of Arth within the boundaries of Dharm.
