## 4. Antiquity and History of Mandir based Arthavyavastha

*When the first structures were built to house the icons, they were probably built of perishable materials like wood, thatch or mud. The structure of many early Hindu mandirs' points to their wood and thatch origins. The roof of the Draupadi Ratha at Mahabalipuram shows clear resemblance to a thatch roof. Similarly, many ancient and medieval mandirs in Karnataka and other states have ceilings which look like crossed wooden beams, bearing signs to their wooden origins.*

\- How Old is The Hindu Temple?, 24 May 2017 by Pankaj Saxena, indiafacts.org

*This does not mean that mandirs were not built before this time. Remnants of a Mauryan-era, brick- and-stone structure believed to be a mandir have been excavated in Bairat district in Rajathan and dated to the 3rd century BCE, and a similar oval, brick temple plan has been excavated at Besnagar, Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh dated to the 2nd Century BCE.*

\- India's Oldest Surviving Mandirs, Anshika Jain, 5 November 2019, livehistoryindia.com

Bharat has mandirs from time immemorial. Mandir based arthavyavastha was active from the time of inception of mandirs. "Applying the resources perspective to a mandir, a mandir does indeed need all the four types of resources. It needs human resources such as the priests, helpers, cooking staff, support staff, cleaning and maintenance staff, singers, musicians, etc. It also needs someone to supervise the collection and employment of funds, someone to take care of the belongings of the deity and so on. In fact, the physical mandir structure and the deities are also physical resources. It needs financial resources to fund the consumables - naivedya, oil, food, abhisheka dravya etc. Finally, it needs information resources or knowledge resources such as the scriptural reference for rituals, mantras to be used and so on." (Temple Management in the Agama-s, 2021 by Dr Deepa Duraiswamy, Notion Press)

At every step of unfolding of a mandir, from its inception till puja started, it impacted arth or economy. Beautiful part is that the model was such that the aarthic activity related to mandir kept rising because the activity linked to the mandir were numerous and they kept growing in scale with passage of time. And as mentioned earlier, some of the oldest cities in the world with continuous habitation are Varanasi, Ujjain, Madurai, Pushkar etc. None known for their industry but all of them known for their Mandirs. Arthavyavastha centred around Mandirs have sustained cities for thousands of years. Following is an example of unfolding of step-by-step mandir based arthavyavastha from the time of construction by K A Nilakanta Sastri:

The mandir was not merely a place of worship; it filled a large place in the cultural and economic life of the people.

<!-- page 26 -->

32

Its construction and maintenance offered employment to numbers of architects and craftsmen who vied with one another in bold planning and skilful execution. The making of icons in stone and metal gave scope to the talents of the best sculptors of the country, some of the larger bronzes cast in the Chola period take their place among the wonders of the world for the mass of metal manipulated as well as for the grace of form attained in the result.

The daily routine, especially of the larger mandirs, gave constant employment to numbers of priests, choristers, musicians, dancing-girls, florists, cooks and many other classes of servants.

The periodical festivals were occasions marked by fairs, contests of learning, wrestling matches and every other form of popular entertainment.

Schools and hospitals were often located in the mandir precincts and it also served often as the town hall where people assembled to consider local affairs or to hear the exposition of sacred literature.

The large endowments in land and cash bestowed on each mandir by successive generations of pious donors tended to make it at once a generous landlord and a banker whose aid was always available to those that needed it.

The practice of decorating images, particularly those used during processions, with numerous jewels set with precious stones encouraged the jeweller's art to a considerable extent.

There can be no better record of the details of the economy of a large mandir than is provided by the numerous inscriptions of the Great Mandir of Tanjore. There the gifts of Rajaraja came largely from booty captured in successful warfare and included well over 41,500 kalanjus of gold, or, taking a kalanju to be about 70 grains, well over 500 lbs. troy weight. The value of jewels was 10,200 kasus, equal to half as many kalanjus in gold. Of silver he gave 50,650 kalanjus or over 600 lbs. troy weight. He set apart lands in villages throughout his dominions, including Ceylon, with an annual income of 116,000 kulams of paddy, equal at the then prevailing prices to 58,000 kasus, besides a cash income of 1,100 kasus. For the service of the mandir, 400 devadasis were impressed from those attached to other mandirs in the empire, each one receiving a panga (share) consisting of a house and one veli of land yielding a net revenue of 100 kalanis of paddy a year. About 180 further such shares were set apart to maintain 212 male dancing masters, musicians, drummers, tailors, goldsmiths, accountants and so on. These men-servants included three people to sing the Ariyam and four others the Tamil which apparently are the two systems of music called ahamargam and desi elsewhere. A choir of 50, on a daily wage of three kurunis of paddy, recited the Tiruppadiyam to the accompaniment of musical instruments. This choir had the additional privilege of filling vacancies by co-option if any of their number died or emigrated without

---

33

leaving behind a suitable relative to take his place. Rajarija's elder sister Kundavai was another generous contributor to mandir funds. On one occasion she presented gold weighing nearly 10,000 kalanjus and utensils valued at 18,000 kasus. Others too - queens high officials and regiments of soldiers - made gifts which have been recorded with equal care and precision on the walls and pillars of the mandir. Cash endowments, which amounted to several thousands of kasus, were loaned to numerous villages assemblies at rates of interest fixed in kind or money, and generally about 12 per cent per annum. Camphor, cardamom-seeds, champak-buds and khus-khus roots were among the products provided for by means of cash endowments.

The inscriptions contain accurate and detailed descriptions of numerous icons, some of which were cast in the form of complex groups of figures illustrating favourite themes from legends. They also contain an equally minute and complete account of the ornaments and jewels of the mandir, and record periodical inquests into the management of mandir affairs by officers of state, and sometimes even by the king himself-clear proof that the business side of the mandir administration was properly controlled. All systems of public administration were not as efficient as the Chola system, and all mandirs were not so well off as that of Tanjore. As a matter of course, however, every mandir held more or less the same position in relation to its neighbourhood that the Great Mandir held in the Chola capital; the difference was only one of degree. And it is no exaggeration to say that the mandir gathered round itself all that was best in the arts of civilized existence and regulated them with the humaneness born of the spirit of dharma. As an agency of social well-being the medieval Bhartiya mandir has few parallels. (A History of South India, 1955 by K A Nilakanta Sastri, Oxford University Press)

### Case Study - II: Meenakshi Amman Mandir as Nucleus of Development

Our Mandirs were fountainhead of knowledge. Only around our mandirs, great cities developed. Meenakshi Amman Mandir at Madurai is not just another mandir. It is a masterpiece of engineering, sculpture, painting etc. Following is a glimpse of some of its high points.

- The Meenakshi Sundareswarar (Bhagwan Shiva is called the beautiful one Sundara+Eswara) mandir is in the centre of the Madurai town. The streets are arranged in squares within squares, keeping the mandir at the heart of the city. Ancient Tamil literature compared this plan to a lotus.
- Each street carries the name of a Tamil month. That means goddess will be taken through that street during that particular month. Now it has changed slightly.

## 5. Mandir - The Nucleus of Arthavyavastha

*There is some special feature associated with the worship in each mandir. For instance, the special feature of Tirumalai is the offering of wealth which takes the form of dropping cash or jewels in the hundi. In Palani, people carry and offer kavadi. At Rameswaram, the bathing of the deity with water brought from the Ganges is considered sacred. In the West Coast, each mandir has its special form of offering. At Ambalapuzha, the offering to Sri Krishna takes the form of pal payasam. The favourite offering to Sri Mahadeva at Vaikom is the conduct of feasts, at which hundreds of people are fed sumptuously. During the annual festival at another Sri Krishna mandir, boat races are conducted in the water course in front of the mandir. At Tripprayar, where the presiding deity is Sri Ramachandra, offerings take the form of detonation - a number of cylinders, packed with gun-powder, are set fire to and they explode one after another in quick succession with a loud report (athir vettu). The sound of athir vettu reverberates from the mandir all round the clock. At Ettumanur, money is offered, as is being done at Tirumalai. At Trichur, ghee offered by devotees, is poured over the deity, with the result that the deity remains practically hidden under the solidified ghee.... the accumulated ghee within the sanctum sanctorum is removed periodically and this ghee, often a hundred years old, purchased by Ayurvedic Physicians, as purana ghritam (old ghee) is a specific for skin disease.*

- Temple Rituals, Shri Shankaracharya Swamigal of Kanchi Kaamakoti Peeta, Temple in India, Vivekananda Kendra Patrika

## Mandir Towns / Cities

Bharat is full of mandir towns or cities. Towns or cities developed because of mandirs. These cities can be broadly classified into 3 categories, which are as following:

A. Mandirs were at the centre of the city and the city developed around them.
B. The city developed because of lot of Mandirs.
C. City Centred round a single cult centre or a Tirtha.

**A. Mandirs were at the centre of the city and the city developed around them.** In such cases, mandir is always built first and is at the centre and the city is built around. In earlier chapter we have already seen example of Madurai developing as a city around Meenakshi Mandir. Now let us look at another example, that of Thanjavur. R Champaklakshmi highlights the key feature of this mandir town as:

With the mandir as its centre, the city of Thanjavur emerged in the following pattern. It consisted of an Ullalai (inner quadrangle around the mandir), for the residences of the priestly, administrative and other elite groups, and a purambadi (an outer circuit) demarcated respectively for the living quarters (streets) of other professional groups, including the nagarams and their angadis, for the palace servants (velams), retinues of the royal family (parivara), all of which were named after the raja and members of the royal family.

Royalty requisitioned employees from various parts of the kingdom (Colamandalam and other mandalams) to serve the mandir and thereby colonise the city. Musicians numbering forty-eight to recite/sing the hymns (patikam), dancing girls (talippendi) numbering four hundred, dance masters, drummers, parasol bearers, lamp lighters, and craftsmen like tailors, braziers, goldsmiths and even astrologers, were brought to Thanjavur. Brahmanas as mandir servants and accountants also came from various centres. By the time the mandir construction reached its final stages, a veritable colonisation had taken place, indicating the implanting of a royal city, including a series of army contingents. Many were given house sites and lands for their maintenance.' The peasantry and artisans who supplied the city with ritual furniture and services in general lived in the villages in the surrounding countryside. Many shepherd families of Thanjavur and other centres were entrusted with the huge livestock donated to the temple. The brisk commerce of Thanjavur was conducted by the four markets (angadis) and nagarattar, while itinerant traders like the Kongavdlar interacted with them. "The distinctive character of Thanjavur as a city derives from the fact that it was a planted city-that it was created by a deliberate act of royal polity in imitation of a sacred bhakti centre with the mandir as its nucleus, to sanctify which the royal author got hymns composed by the royal preceptor, and, finally, that it was at once the product and symbol of the socio-cultural milieu of the Cola period. (Trade Ideology and Urbanisation, 1996 by R Champaklakshmi, Oxford University Press)

The urban planning was centred around our mandir and importance of aarthic activity

---

in relation to mandir also played a significant role in the layout of the town.

**B. The city developed because of lot of Mandirs.** Though there is one core or principal mandir, it is not the centre of the city. "Kudamukku-Palaiyarai and Kancipuram may be classified as multi-mandir centres evolving after centuries of growth from earlier agrarian clusters, each mandir, which marked their growth, representing the locus of the ceremonial complex at different chronological points, thus leading to the emergence of dispersed ceremonial/sacred centres, rather than compact ones like Tanjavur." (Trade Ideology and Urbanisation, 1996 by R Champaklakshmi, Oxford University Press)

More than thousand-year-old, city known for its mandirs, Bhubaneswar is still alive and kicking. 'A mandir town with series of ancient sandstone mandirs, heritage ponds and water tanks, its wealth of monuments is testament to an ancient continuous architectural and historical heritage covering over 2,000 years from the 3rd century BCE to the 15th century CE representing most of the important dynastic changes over the period. Bhubaneswar is dubbed the "Temple City" - a nom-de-plume earned because of the 700 temples which once stood here. It still boasts of a cluster of magnificent mandirs, constituting virtually a complete record of Kalinga architecture almost from its nascence to its culmination.' (whc.unesco.org)
