Our Mandirs are the nucleus of all these facets, and hence their impact on Arthavyavastha is being considered as a part of mandir based Arthavyavastha.

## A. Karmakaand Samskara (rituals) based Arthavyavastha

*Our enlightened ancestors, the maharishis, blessed us with the Agama Shastra that prescribes the performance of various rituals. As a sugar-coated capsule of medicine is given to a patient to keep him healthy, our ancestors prescribed the rituals, festivals and celebrations by keeping the Mandir as the centre of a town, village or a city. A layman may follow these instructions in blind faith with due respect to the elders of his parental generation. But when we contemplate deeply on the subtle purpose of these rituals, we arrive at the love and affection that our ancestors had towards the entire creation, the human race, our planet, its environment and finally our safe future.*

- Tirumala: Sacred food of God, 2016 by A V Ramana Dikshitulu and Kota Neelima, Lustre

Flowers hold a special place in Bhartiya culture as they are intrinsic to many customs and rituals. Flowers adorn our lives from birth to death. References to flowers and gardens are found in ancient history books and Sanskrit classics like the Rig Veda, Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Sarangdhara. It is mentioned in the works of Shudraka, Kalidasa etc. In Kalidas's Abhijnana Shankuntalam, when Shakuntala first appears on stage, her friend describes her to be as dainty as a jasmine. Offering flowers in mandirs is an important ritual.

The fragrance from Delhi's Ghazipur flower market fills the Vaishno Devi Mandir premises which is adorned with thousands of roses, dahlias, orchids and strings of marigolds this Navratri festival. Representatives from the market said that flowers worth three crores rupees are sent in two batches to deck up the entrance to the bhawan and the main Bhawan. According to data shared by the market, 18,000 bundles of roses, 22,000 bundles of gerbera, 7000 bundles of orchids, 6000 bundles of anthurium, 10,000 bundles of lilies apart from other flowers, including marigold strings are sent in two batches. As many as 350 to 400 persons are sent from Delhi to decorate the bhawan. Not only Vaishno Devi, but even other mandirs like Kangra Devi and Jwala Devi mandirs are also decorated with flowers from this market. (Flowers from Ghazipur market adorn Vaishno Devi Temple, 6 October 2019, business-standard.com)

## Case Study - I: Jasmine Flower and Madurai

*The malligai has been depicted in the sculptures of the Pallava dynasty monuments at Mahabalipuram and Kanchipuram, and in the Chalukya dynasty temple at Pattadakkaln in Karnataka. In the Hall of the Thousand Pillars temple, two Tanjavur style painting which represents the Meenakshi kalyanam (wedding) and Meenakshi pattabhishekam (coronation). Both these portray the deity adorned with malligai garlands. Jasmine buds are even today an important part of jewellery design in Bharat.*

- Madurai Malligai: Madurai and its Jasmine A celebration, 2017 by Dr Uma Kannan, Thiagarajar Publication

---

83

Ritual of offering flowers in puja, to many may look insignificant, in spiritual, scientific as well as aarthic terms. And if you also think so then you will be surprised.

Jasmine flowers association with Devi Meenakshi and the city of Madurai is since inception.

Devi Meenakshi at the Meenakshi Amman Mandir, Madurai, loves malligai so much that she is decorated with the Jasmine flower six times a day. From her garlands to the decorations on her yaali, to her poopallakku (floral palanquin) everything is decorated with malligai. Jasmine is also on Meenakshi's thirumangalyam (nuptial pendant). According to the traditions of this unique nuptial, it is Devi Meenakshi who receives the hand of Bhagwan Sundareswarar. (In Hindu custom the groom receives the hand of the bride.)

The huge demand for Jasmine for use in mandir across Bharat makes it a commercial crop. Malligai is commercial cultivated in Coimbatore, Madurai, Dindigul, Athoor, Nilakottai, Tirumangalam, Kallupalli and Thiruparankundrum (Tamil Nadu); Bangalore, Ballary, Mysore and Kolar (Karnataka); Pune, Aurangabad and Ahmednagar (Maharashtra); Ahmedabad, Anand and Vadodara (Gujarat); Ambala, Gurgaon and Faridabad (Haryana); Kannauj, Jaunpur and Gazipur (Uttar Pradesh); Delhi, Ludhiana, Jalandhar, Patiala and Amritsar (Punjab); Ranaghat, Kolaghat, Panskura and 24-Parganas (West Bengal); Udaipur, Ajmer, Jaipur and Kota (Rajasthan); Hoja, Jorhat, Alnugarh (Assam). However, largest chunk of areas under jasmine flower production is in TamilNadu and Karnataka. It is an ideal crop for small farmers whose land holdings are less than 1 acre.

If it is grown in so many parts of Bharat, then why is only Devi at Madurai fond of malligai? Because, malligai grown in Madurai is special. Dr Uma Kannan cites four distinctive features of Madurai Malligai, which are as follows:

i. Fragrance: The fragrance of the Madurai malligai has been known to last for thirty-six hours. The laterite and reddish soils, a distinctive feature of the Madurai district, are rich in sulphur, which is the secret behind the fragrance causing alkaloids in jasmine; jasmone and alpha terpinol.

ii. Petals: Compared to other varieties of jasmine grown in various parts of the country, the Madurai malligai has thicker petals that allow the flowers to retain moisture and delay the process of withering. They also give the flowers some firmness, and this makes it easier to weave them in various patterns and into garlands.

iii. Colour: The Madurai malligai is greenish white when it is picked from the plant early in the morning. After a few hours, it turns milky white and then a shiny creamy white during the evening.

iv. Freshness: Normally, the jasmine that is grown in other parts of the country blooms before or around 5 pm. But the Madurai malligai blooms only after 6 or 7 pm. And it

<!-- page 52 -->

84

stays fresh longer the next morning because it blooms later in the evening.

(Madurai Malligai: Madurai and its Jasmine A Celebration, 2017 by Dr Uma Kannan, Thiagarajar Publication)

Next question, why Devi Meenakshi is more found of Malligai than Bhagwan Sundareswarar? Again, the reason is scientific.

The generation of flower sellers have developed their own traditional knowledge system. The whole process from field to being offered to Devi for puja or being used by a lady on her hair, is completely eco-friendly. "Custom is at the root of everything the flower sellers do, even the way they string and measure the flowers and fix the rates. The fibrous outer sheath of the banana stem is dried, rolled into 'skeins' and sold to flower vendors, who slit them into thin strings. These are moistened to prevent them from breaking and then used to tie flowers. There are numerous styles of weaving, knitting and knotting the jasmine. Some of the techniques of weaving are Uruttu Kattu (unique to Madurai), Pattai kattu, Saathaa kattu, Maalai, Thumbihai maalai, Nilai aalai, and Thirumbi-p-paar (originating in Madurai).

Traditional palm leaf basket is used for transporting Jasmine buds. Flower sellers wrap flowers for their customers to carry home in a piece of banana leaf and secure it with a

twist of banana fibre, an age-old custom that's eco-friendly and aesthetically pleasing too. Jute bags are used for transporting (large quantities) the soft white blooms because they are porous and allow the jasmine bud to breath and retain their freshness longer". (Madurai Malligai: Madurai and its Jasmine A Celebration, 2017 by Dr Uma Kannan, Thiagarajar Publication)

## B. Prasad based Arthavyavastha

*Food offerings require good harvests, which in turn, require high agricultural activity. The food, after it is offered to Bhagwan is distributed among assembled devotees irrespective of caste, creed, gender, age and social status. The sacred food or prasadam is, in fact, a happy event of daily feeding the community to take care of each other as human beings with divine guidance. The purpose of our ancestors in setting up this beautiful ritual is thus achieved when the devotee gets the blessings of God in the form of the prasadam.*

- Tirumala: Sacred food of God, 2016 by A V Ramana Dikshitulu and Kota Neelima, Lustre

Prasad is a factor of local produce, seasonality, nutritive requirement of the body according to the astha prahar, and above all bhakti bhav i.e., on arthavyavastha, ayurveda and adhyatam. Apart from this, fuel and utensil also impact the prasad and each mandir has its own prescribed norms for the same.

Different fuel is used in different mandir for cooking

| Mandir | Fuel |
|---|---|
| Guruvayoor | Husk of coconut for cooking for Bhagwan |
| | Tamarind bark for cooking for the devotees |
| Govindji Maharaj (Imphal) | Rice husk |
| Titupati | Wood from Mango or Palash tree |

Tatiyasthan in Vrindavan and Jagannath Mandir at Puri use clay utensils. Otherwise, copper, brass, and bronze are used, while steel and aluminium are shunned.

Please do note that the above-mentioned trees and the art of making utensils from different metals survive due to offering of prasad in our mandirs.

Just for the records, In 1960s - a staggering 70,000 of varieties were available (Tamilnadu). Ironically as paddy cultivation was scaled up through hybrids, by 1991, over 75 per cent of India's rice production was coming from less than 10 varieties. (Nine Rupees An Hour, 2019 by Aparna Karthikeyan).

---

Steve Jobs of Apple used to walk seven mile every Sunday to the Hare Krishna Iskcon Mandir, to have a proper meal. This is the story of lakhs of devotees. Prasad offering has redefined humanity and has impacted arthavyavastha also. Prasad has given birth to fast food restaurants much before multinational companies entered Bharat. Udupi hotels are a product of mandir.

*Udupi hotels began in the 1920s and 30s in Madras. The menu was divided into meals and tiffin corresponding to the heavy and light meals served in the temple. Then items were cooked in large pots in a separate room at the back of the hotel. They were doled out into smaller stainless-steel buckets and served by servers in a style reminiscent of mass feeding in the temples. And within twenty minutes or so the space was being readied for the next lot of customers. Udupi Brahmins successfully adapted the mass feeding and pilgrim management in the mandir to a model of catering and hoteliering.* (Turmeric Nation: A passage through India's Tastes, 2020 by Shylashri Shankar, Speaking Tiger Books)

## Case Study - II: Prasad at Tirumala

One of the most famous prasad is from Tirumala. It is centuries old tradition and inscriptions talk about its contribution to the arthavyavastha of Tirupati.

From inscription it appears that a lucrative prasadam trade began in the mandir as the quantity of daily offerings returned to the donor and the mandir functionaries far exceeded what could be consumed by them. Pilgrims visiting the mandir also desired to receive the prasadam for themselves and their family members who could not attend the mandir. From inscriptional evidence, it appears mandir functionaries and donors would turn their prasadam shares over to a group of 11 vendors (prasadakkar) who would subsequently sell the prasadam to visiting pilgrims. On average, it appears that a typical donation would return a total annual return of 10% (split as described above: 25% to the donor and 75% to mandir functionaries). The prasadakkar would pay a lease fee to the mandir functionary or donor in exchange for the ability to sell the prasadam to pilgrims at a profit. Based on inscriptions designating the right of the donor to transfer their prasadam share to a prasadakkarar, the prasadam trade was not illegal nor did it have negative connotations. The entire system was closely supervised by the Sthanattars. The leasing of prasadam sales allowed for the mandir functionaries and the donors to monetize their share. Additionally, it appears that the mandir functionaries (including the archakas) and donors became quite wealthy from the prasada trade and had a substantial financial interest in continuing to make village or monetary endowments. As a result, the Tiruapti town developed a vibrant and affluent economy fuelled by the prasadam trade. These donations allowed for grand worship within the mandir, but also provided a steady investments income. Thus, the proportion of donations made by mandir functionaries (including priests) and local

<!-- page 54 -->

88

merchants and citizens grew substantially between 1509 and 1568. (The Priests of Tirumala, 2015 by Sridhar V Basavaraju)

Prasad's contribution to arthavyavastha at Tirumala is age old and it continues till date. Following is the current state of Tirupati Laddu:

When, there were no hotels at Tirumala and the prasad given by the mandir was the only source of food for the pilgrims Apart from praasadam, Tirupati Laddu is famous across the world. As per the Dittam – the 750-gram special laddu should have 23.5 grams of cashew, 12.5 grams of raisins, 8.2 grams almonds and 6.2 grams of sugar candy. The moisture content should be only 12%.

In their 2016-17 budget, the mandir board estimated the revenue from laddus sales was Rs 175 crore. Officials of the mandir board said that about two crore laddus were sold in 2015, and they expect the sales in 2016 to go up to three crore.

Till about 10 years ago, the laddus were made inside the Srivari mandir. A generous donation by a devotee in 2006 helped the trust set up mechanised kitchens in the complex. For 22 hours a day, workers at the kitchen are busy kneading gram flour, cashew nuts, raisins, sugar, cardamom and ghee to dish out about three lakh mouth-watering Tirupati Laddus. Here, 200 Brahmin priests stand along a 500 X 30 feet steel table, making the laddus under. About 600 mandir employees and 200 Srivari Sevaks (volunteers) are involved in marketing the laddu in temple complex. (How the Tirupati Laddu was marketed to bring sweet returns for Tirumala mandir, GS Radhakrishna, 31 October 2016, scroll.in)

One can imagine the volume of ingredients consumed and their impact on arthvyavastha. Making of prasad at Tirupati has kept pace with time without losing its piousness. What is demonstrated above is example of just one mandir. Prasad of every mandir is sought after. Prasad creates its own arthavyavastha using local ingredients.

### C. Shilpkala (Craft) based Arthavyavastha

*Temples across India have always encouraged art. For centuries now, murals (paintings on rock or stone walls and ceilings), art on palm leaves, papier mache, textiles, exquisite metal crafts and other handicrafts have been made by artisans who lived around the temples. Much of the religious art, until date, is inspired by the deities and the legends of the gods and goddesses of temple towns. Whenever we visit a temple, it is important that we observe the art and crafts in its surroundings - for the art in each temple has a story to tell.*

\- Temple Tales, 2019 by Sudha G Tilak, Hachette India

Shilpa refers to art and craft while Shastra means science. Together, Shilpa Shastra means the science of art and crafts. Shilpa covers every aspect of art and culture that includes sculptor, potter, perfumer, painter, weaver, architect, dancer, musician and countless others. Shilp Shastra is an umbrella term for numerous Hindu texts that describe arts, crafts, and their design rules, principles and standards. There are sixty-

---

89

four Kala (arts) i.e., 64 Shilpkalas. The list of 64 Shilpkalas vary from period to period, scripture to scripture. It covers almost every aspect of mandir construction. From there it moved to masses and became Hastkala. Hastkala is part of Shilpkala. Hastkala became handicraft in English. Hence Bharatiya handicrafts are rooted in our Mandirs and Hindutva. They are as ancient as one can go back in time. Most importantly they are not mere crafts, they are part of rituals. Following is a list of few of the handicrafts from some states of Bharat, depicting their linkage with Mandir and Hindutva.

### Andhra Pradesh

- *Allagadda Stone Craft:* Allagadda Stone Craft dates back to 2nd Century BCE and statue of Devi and Devatas are carved on sand stone.

- *Bobbili Veena:* Bobbili Veena is a large plucked string instrument used in Carnatic classical music. The Veena is named after Bobbili, a place where it was invented. A Bobbili Veena is carved from a single piece of jack wood.

- *Budithi Bell:* Budithi Bell and Brass Craft are the products made out of alloy like brass in Budithi, a village in Srikakulam district.

- *Cheriyal Paintings:* The scroll paintings are traditionally painted on a khadi cloth after the fabric is processed with sawdust, tamarind-seed paste, rice starch, white mud and tirumani, or tree gum. The canvas is allowed to dry and the priming process is repeated once, after which it is ready to use once dry. The art form involved paintings that depicted scenes from the Hindu history like Ramayan and Mahabharat and also stories that were meant to educate the village folks. After the scrolls were painted, the scrolls were pinned in the background and the artistes danced and sang to every narrative painted on the scroll. Storytellers considered these paintings holy and as part of their religious customs, used to immerse them in water after performances. Very few paintings from 17th and 18th century survived this custom and exist today.

- *Durgi Stone Craft:* Durgi stone carvings date back to 3rd century CE and idols of Devi and Devatas are carved from soft lime stone.

- *Etikoppaka Bommalu:* Located on the banks of the river Varaha in Vishakhapatnam district, is a small village called Etikoppaka. Here toys and Baranis (wooden boxes) are made out of wood and painted with lacquer color and are traditionally known as Etikoppaka toys or Etikoppaka Bommalu. Boxes are made to contain various items to be offered to Bhagwan.

- *Sri Kalahasti Woodcarvings:* Classic pieces like Vaikunta Dwaram, Sri Krishna Tulabharam, Gali Gopuram, Radha Krishna in the cradle, Vinayaka in different shapes among others are carved by the artisans. Red sandal wood of Chittoor district is used to carve out images of Bhagwan Venkateswara and of the Tirupati mandir. This wood resists white ants and fire and is hard and elastic.

<!-- page 55 -->

- *Tholu Bommalata*: Tholu means leather in Telugu and bommalu means dolls. This form of art is believed to have originated in 200 BCE during the rule of the Satavahana dynasty. They were instrumental in disseminating knowledge regarding Hindu history such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata and local folk tales, to hinterlands.

### Assam

- *Bamboo Craft*: The art of carving miniature statues of deities on bamboo was introduced during the time of Shri Shankaradeva himself.
- *Mask Making*: Masks were used for religious dance and drama. They were conceptualized as a tool by Shri Shankaradeva to make and depict the characters of Srimad Bhagwat to the devotees.
- *Prayer Towel Gamosa* - The one place where the gamosa attains a higher station is at the namghar, or Vaishnava prayer houses across Assam. Namghars have a shrine called monikut for the deity. This resembles a hill made of tiny steps with the murti inside. The steps are often adorned with the gamosa. The holy book Bhagavata Purana by the 15th-century saint Shri Shankardeva is often placed in namghars on a gamosa. Weavers weave clothes mainly for their own household and will take orders only during festivals such as Durga Puja, Bihu, and Kali Puja

### Bihar

- *Sikki Grass*: In Bihar and UP the grass has served as a vital raw material in making of a variety of products since ancient times. There is hardly a ritual where it is not taken into account, figures of deities and votive offerings are woven during festivals, young women weave baskets known as 'Pauthi' which are used to exchange gifts in a wedding.
- *Mithila Painting*: Mithila Painting was first done by Devi Gauri. Bhagwan Ram broke the famous bow of Bhagwan Shiv 'Pinaka' to win the princess's hand in Sita's swayamvar. At that time, Devi Gauri, Bhagwan Shiv's wife expressed her desire to paint the first ever Mithila painting on the wall 'Ramcharitmanas', has a mention of the incident on the occasion of Ram and Sita's wedding ceremony. Now a days, scenes from Ramayan, Mahabharat etc are depicted in the painting.

### Gujarat

- *Applique*: Applique and reverse applique both are also sometimes combined with chain stitch and herringbone stitch embroidery. Applique is the art of layering small pieces of fabric cut in various shapes on to a base fabric. Bhagwan Ganesh is very often represented through this method on applique friezes to be placed on top of doorways. From episodes in the epics like

Ramayana, to animals like elephants, peacocks, parrots, flowers to even modern day to day objects like watches and music players, all feature in the colourful pieces of applique.

- *Mata ni Pachedi*: Mata ni pachedi literally means "behind the mother goddess." It is a cloth that constitutes a mandir of the Devi.
- *Sankheda Furniture*: A craft tradition so deeply inherent in the collective identity of the practitioners, that their town is named after it. Sankheda, a small town in the eastern region of Gujarat derives its name from 'sanghedu', the word for a lathe in the Gujarati language. Sankheda furniture is considered auspicious and is used in many religious and festive occasions.

### Himachal Pradesh

- *Chamba Rumal*: Earliest reported form of this rumal is the one made by Bebe Nanaki, sister of Guru Nanak in the 16th century, which is now preserved in the Gurudwara at Hoshiarpur. Chamba Rumal is now made in square and rectangular shapes

### Karnataka

- *Sutrada Gombeyata*: Here the word 'Sutra' connotes string. The term 'gombeyata' is meant to imply dancing. These puppet shows are performed in front of the Devi Kali's mandir.
- *Yakshagana Gombeyata*: The word 'Yakshagana' connoting 'the song of the celestial beings. These puppet shows are also performed in front of the Devi Kali's mandir.
- *Ilkal Saree*: The pallu of the Ilkal saree (the part worn over the shoulder) carries designs of mandirs.
- *Mysore Paintings*: The artisans excelled at painting murals on the walls of mandirs built by the rajas of this region. In the 17th and 18th centuries, this became a formal style of art under Krishnaraja Wodeyar. He founded the Mysore School of Art, and also wrote the Sritattvanidhi, a book that listed the styles of drawing Devi and Devatas, the colour schemes and composition, and the designs of the paintings. The paintings were created on walls, wooden boards, and a specific kind of cloth, stiffened using paints

### Madhya Pradesh

- *Bhedaghat Marble Statues*: Bhedaghat is situated on the banks of the Narmada river. Craftsman sit by the ghats of the river and chisel idols of Ganesh, Shiv and Parvati from marble rocks.
- *Khajuraho Metal Craft*: Mandir doors, bells, 'kalash' for the holy water of river Ganga and money containers, are all transformed from their plain, utilitarian forms to the ornamental, with the art of engraving practised by the

<!-- page 56 -->

craftsmen of Khajuraho. Taking inspirations from the carvings of Khajuraho's ancient mandirs, craftsmen draw images directly on the metal vessels. No rough sketches are drawn, no reference guidelines; just the chisel hits the metal and poetry is made onto the golden-brown metal.

- *Tikamgarh Bell Metal Casting:* Tikamgarh, bell metal casting has created canons and war weapons for rajas and soldiers, to bullock carts and cattle bells for the farmer, and real gold decorations for mandir . The process of casting used in Tikamgarh is similar to the Dhokra casting in Betul, as both the crafts take shape with lost wax casting, a common process used to cast objects in metals. But while the Dhokra of Betul is created with strings of wax on individual pieces, in Tikamgarh, the metal pieces are sculpted in the usual way and moulds are created to replicate the objects.

- *Budni Ghat Wood Craft:* On the banks of river Narmada, is Budni Ghat, where soft wood spins on the lathe from morning to twilight, metamorphosing into beautiful objects and shapes. These objects were earlier made from Sagwan wood (Teak), but as the wood became rarer, the craftsmen switched to the locally available small pieces of Dudhi wood, which is soft and easy to carve and being light in colour, it makes the lacquer hues glow.

**Maharashtra:**

- *Narayan Peth Saree:* These sarees come from the Solapur. Characterized by broad borders and vibrant colours, the body of the saree has small motifs, in the shape of rudrakshas.

**Manipur:**

- *Morang Phee Saree:* Morang is the saree with a mandir border.

**Odisha**

- *Chhau:* Chhau is a dance of wars and has steps resembling a martial art performance. It has the merits of 'Nritta' or nature of 'Tandav' as described in the 'Natyashastra' of Bharat. Stories of from Ramayana, Mahabharata and Purana are portrayed in the dance.

- *Suta Luga:* Suta luga (cotton weaves) single count cotton fabrics are woven in Jagatsingpur. Symbolic Mandir and Rudraksha patterns are designed in the cloth using thread work.

- *Filigree:* "Cuttacki Tarkasi", the silver filigree of Odisha is world renowned for its delicate artistry and brilliant craftsmanship. The process of making a silver filigree product is very peculiar in character; for it does not involve carving, engraving or moulding a block of metal into jewellery, rather, building the piece bit by bit, by joining hair thin silver wires. Designs are first drafted on a piece of paper, inspirations for which are derived from mandirs, the Konark

wheel, gods and goddesses, flora and fauna. Jewellery is just one of the beautiful objects of desire that the craftsmen make with filigree, along with idols of Devi and Devatas, decorative animals and replicas of mandirs.

- *Applique Work:* Applique work comes from Pipli village, which was established by the Raja of Odisha for the craftsmen who made applique umbrellas and canopies for the annual Jagannath Yatra. A craft that originated as a mandir art now finds its application in a wide range of household, decorative and ceremonial products.

**Rajasthan**

- *Kathputli:* Kathputli shows are created with 'kath'. Kath connotes wooden and 'putli' means doll. These dolls have cotton stuffed in their hands and are manipulated by a few strings which are attached to them. These storytellers mostly have their roots in the nomadic puppeteer community of nat bhats.

- *Stone Sculpture:* About 250 years ago, Sawai Jai Singh II summoned these sculptors to Jaipur for their skill, as he shifted the operating capital of his empire from Amer to Jaipur. **At that time sculpture making was seen as a forte of the Brahmins, who were believed to be descendants of Atri Rishi.** They were specifically commissioned because of the religious significance of the sculptures of deities. But today, an overwhelming 4 to 5 thousand people from across the boundaries of various cast and creed are pursuing this ingenious art here.

- *Pichwai Painters:* Pichwai painting are works of art that are used to adorn the walls of mandirs, behind the idol. The Pichwai style is from the Nathdwara School, and is identified by characteristic features of large eyes, broad nose and a heavy body, similar to the features on the idol of Shrinathji. Themes such as Raas Leela, Holi, Annakut (Special food prepared for Govardhan puja) are also seen on relevant occasions.

- *Kaavad:* It is a travelling shrine containing within its doors elaborate tales and epics. With the mystery of a new turn in the tale behind every door, the Kaavad would leave the audiences spellbound. The Kaavad shrine is made of mango or sheesham wood.

**Tamil Nadu:**

- *Mandir Jewellery:* Deities in mandirs are adorned in brilliant gemstones and shining gold jewellery. Classical dancers also wear jewels that are modelled after the ones that adorn the mandir murtis. Hence the term mandir jewellery. Vadasery, in Nagarcoil in Kanyakumari, is the hub for hereditary artisans and goldsmiths who make mandir jewellery. They design jewels that adorn mandir deities and for Bharatanatyam dancers to wear. Made of silver and coated in

<!-- page 57 -->

gold and studded with gemstones, these jewels look resplendent. Mandir jewellery is also worn by Tamil brides on their wedding day, much like the divine maiden who stands in eternal wait for her groom in Kanyakumari.

### West Bengal

- *Baluchari Saree:* Baluchar Village of Baranagar in Murshidabad is famous for the terracotta panels of the 18th-century Char Bangla Mandir. The terracotta panels portray scenes from the two great epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. The Murshidabad silks, called Baluchari, are famous for depicting the panels of these mandirs. The silk saree, have borders and motifs of scenes from the Ramayana, Krishna Lila and the Shakti Purana beautifully woven into them.

- *Kantha:* Kantha is perhaps the oldest forms of Bhartiya embroidery as it can be traced back to the first and second CE. The thought behind this needlework was to reuse old clothes and materials and turn them into something new. This is what makes kantha embroidery only one of its kind.

- *Dhokra Damar Metal Sculptures:* Long before faster and cheaper methods of making products came into being, Bengal's Dhokra Damar the traditional metal-smith tribes carved on wax to make bell metal sculptures. They are nomads. Their detailed depictions of Devi and Devatas, intricate lamps, bells and ornaments were greatly revered. 'Shilpshastra' mentions this art and it was practised in Indus Valley. Before any artisan sits to make the figure, he prays for guidance from Tvastram (son of Bhagwan Vishwakarma), said to be an expert in metal alloys.

### Case Study - III: Handicraft an important source of Additional Income

Handicrafts have significant impact on the aarthic life of artisans. A study "Status of Tribal Handicraft - an option for livelihood of tribal community in the states of Arunachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttaranchal and Chhattisgarh" conducted by Socio-Economic and Educational Development Society (SEEDS), and Sponsored by Planning Commission Government of India in 2006, presented the following findings:

- The Khampt (Khampties of Lohit) makes beautiful religious images, figures of dancers, toys and other objects.
- Woodcraft from the tribal belt of Bastar is known for figures of deities, and Bell metal artifacts. Most of the products are dharmik items (Danteswari, Shitala mata, Mankali mata, Bhanodeo etc).
- Craftsmen of Rajasthan also make delicately carved figures of deities on rosewood and sandalwood.
- In the woodcraft of Uttranchal, the mifs, ordinarily of the Devi and Devtas, add to the richness of the carvings.

Due to subsistence economy, most of the tribals work as daily wager or indulge into small scale handicraft activities or farming in the small piece of land or collect forest product from nearby areas. In majority of cases, handicraft is considered as part time occupation or tertiary activity in economic ladder. The revenue generated from handicraft has substantial share of total household income. During the survey, it has been observed that it constitutes more than 30% of total household income as shown in the Table - 1. Some of the important findings are below:

**Income in ₹ from various sources (Table - 1)**

| STATE | Districts | Income from farming | Income from daily wages | Income from Handicraft | Total Income |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arunachal Pradesh | Lower Subansiri | 700 | 450 | 2150 | 3300 |
| | Papum Pare | 500 | 600 | 2100 | 3200 |
| Chattisgarh | Dantewada | 1900 | 1000 | 1300 | 4200 |
| | Jagdal Pur | 1600 | 700 | 1500 | 3800 |
| | Raigarh | 1600 | 1600 | 500 | 3700 |
| Rajasthan | Banswara | 600 | 2100 | 1500 | 4200 |
| | Dungarpur | 600 | 2600 | 1300 | 4500 |
| | Udaipur | 600 | 2000 | 1300 | 3900 |
| Uttranchal | Chamoli | 1100 | 900 | 1100 | 3100 |
| | Pithoragarh | 1100 | 300 | 1500 | 2900 |
| | Uttarkashi | 600 | 1000 | 1800 | 3400 |

In Arunachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal, primary income is from sell of handicraft where in case of Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan, the primary income is from daily wages. Despite facing various odds, tribal derive major portion of income from sale of their handicrafts.

Export of handicrafts was USD 2.1 billion for the financial year 2021-22. Most probably ninety percent of it will be mandir craft. The internal consumption will be same if not more.

These handicrafts are designed based on Hindu Dharm, inspired from sculptors from our mandirs and are sold around our mandirs or dharmic fairs. Thus contributing to mandir based arthavyavastha.

## D. Natya, Nritya, Geet and Sangeet (Drama, Dance, Music and Song) based Arthavyavastha

*In Bharat, mandirs were the spaces where dance, poetry, music and the performing arts flourished. Most mandirs had stages or platforms, where performances were held before kings or noblemen. Mandirs across Bharat are linked to dance forms like Bharatanatyam, Kathakali, Odissi and Manipuri. Folk, tribal and street theatre performances were also hosted in and around famous mandirs and during festivals. Similarly, temples are also synonymous with music. Poets and composers often wrote songs in praise of the mandir deity, and their songs carried the names of the gods and mandir towns. Today, dance and music festivals are still held in many mandir precincts, like the Mamallapuram Dance Festival near the Pallava Shore Mandir in Tamil Nadu, the dance festival at the Sun Mandir in Modhera in Gujarat among many others. This speaks volumes of the continuing links between our mandirs and music and dance. In no other country in the world can you find such a strong and continuing connection between music and dance forms and mandirs.*

\- Temple Tales, 2019 by Sudha G Tilak, Hachette India

Bhartrihari in Neeti Shatakam says, human without literature, song and art is like animal without nails and tail. It is blessing for the animals that human beings do not eat grass like them.

सहित्यसङ्गीतकलाविहीनः साक्षात्पशु पुच्छविषाणहीनः।
तृणनखादन्निपिर्जीवमानसत्द्राघेयपरमपशूनाम्॥

Dance, Music, Song and Drama contribute to the aarthic activity and it is fascinating:

### Natya (Drama)

*Natyashastra..is part theatrical manual, part philosophy of aesthetics, part history, part theology. Its goals include providing a precise description of stage construction and equally precise guidelines for the movements, facial expressions, and mudras (often) used synonymously with the term hasta or hand gesture to be used in performance. Natyashastra describes eight rasas, and identifies them as associated with both colours and deities.*

*The design of a theatre in ancient Bharat "was considered a branch of mandir architecture. After all, the Natyashastra describes the performance of a play as a sacrifice to the gods.*

*The form, the gestural language, the structure of the dance, the physical edifice of the mandir and the physical form of the dancer herself become one with the content of the performance, the symbolic, transformative concepts that compose a unique relationship between deity and mandir, mandir and dancer, dancer and dance, dance and spectator. There is emotion, there is cognition, and both are "experienced and discussed as unified activity".*

*The subject matter of the play determined the time of the performance. A play based on*

---

*a tale of virtue was performed before noon; a play rich in instrumental music, unfolding a story of strengthen and energy, in the afternoon; a play of erotic sentiments in the first part of the night; and plays of pathetic sentiments in the fourth part of the night. No plays were presented at midnight, at midday or at the time of evening prayers. Mostly, dramatic performances were held in the afternoon and lasted four or five hours.*

(Rasa: Performing the Divine in India, 2008 by Susan L. Schwartz, Motilal Banarsidas)

Natya based on Ramayan turned around fortunes of Bengali theatre. Girish Chandra Ghosh (28 February 1844 - 8 February 1912) was a musician, poet, playwright, novelist, theatre director and actor. Largely responsible for the golden age of Bengali theatre, he can be referred to as the Father of Bengali Theatre. He co-founded the Great National Theatre, the first Bengali professional theatre company. At National Theatre following several failures with plays by established playwrights, produced his own historical drama Ravana Badh (Slaying of Ravana) on 30 July 1881 and marked a positive turning point in Bengali theatre.

Natya has been kept alive by mandirs through rituals. "The Sri Krishna Mandir at Guruvayur is dedicated to Krishna's endearing avatar as a divine little boy. Each day, the Guruvayur Mandir has a performance called Krishnattam, a traditional dance-drama based on the stories on Krishna's life: his boyhood, his fights with evil demons and many more. It is a brilliant sight as the dancers wear elaborate Kathakali costumes, colourful face paint and dazzling jewels. Krishnattam is based on the eight dramatic plays about Krishna's life and miracles. They are Avataram (birth of Krishna), Kaliamardanam (killing of the poisonous serpent Kalia), Rasakrida (dance of Krishna and gopikas), Kamsavadham (slaying of his uncle, the demon Kamsa), Swayamvaram (Krishna's wedding to Rukmini), Banayuddham (Krishna's battle with the demon Narakasuran), Vividavadham (Krishna's role in the Mahabharata), and Swargaroham (Krishna leaving Earth for Vaikunta or heaven). In most temples, devotees offer fruits, milk or sweets to the deity, but at the mandir of Guruvayur, devotees can choose to offer these dance-dramas! Every day, devotees pay and book various Krishnattam dances as offerings at the mandir hall before a huge brass lamp burning bright, lighting these blessed performances." (Temple Tales, 2019, by Sudha G Tilak, Hachette India) Sponsoring dance drama as offering, there can't be more beautiful way then this to promote and preserve art.

Author could not find separate study to find out the finance and economy of Dance, Song and Drama in Bharat. Unfortunately, they are clubbed as Performing arts industry, which includes vulgar Urduwood dance, music and theatre.

### Case Study - IV: Contribution of Song and Music (Prayer) in Arthavyavastha

Our prayers exist from Vedic period. Prayers are made to nature, river, hill as well as planets. Beauty of our prayers is that it is not bound by any language. One can pray within mind or in any language he or she wishes to. Some prayers are part of rituals and some are exclusively for pujaris. Some are sung individually; some are sung in a group. In the group they take the form of bhajan and kirtan.

When one starts learning prayers, it is best to do so in a group. As devotee evolves, he or she starts praying alone and at some point the devotee does not need words. He or she can connect with the Bhagwan with prayer in his or her mind. There are small prayers, there are long prayers. Some have different names of Bhagwan, some talk about the valour of the Bhagwan. Prayers help individuals to tide over the crisis.

There are prayers common for all Devi, Devta as well as individual prayers for each Bhagwan. Individual prayers cannot be interchanged. Different devi, devtas are called upon for different purposes and different occasions Devi Saraswati and Bhagwan Ganesh are worshipped in schools. Businessmen worship Bhagwan Ganesh, Devi Lakshmi, Bhagwan Vishwakarma and Devi Durga. One can pray to different Devi Devta at different times, in different circumstances as per comfort. Different region, different mandirs will have different prayer for same Devi Devata. There are individual prayers like Hanuman Chalisha to get over the individual fear.

Prayers have lot of power at the same time they contribute significantly to the arthavyavastha. Gulshan Kumar went on to build T-Series on the back of devotional songs alone.

The contribution of dance, song, music and drama originated in our mandirs, to arthavyavastha is massive.

### F. Parikrama (circumambulation) based Arthavyavastha

Parikrama or Pradakshina refers to circumambulation of sacred places to imbibe their energy. There are different types of Pradakshina:

- **Atma Pradakshina**: Going around self. It is performed after daily worship or prayer.
- **Pada Pradakshina**: A person needs to walk on foot (Pada) around the shrine.
- **Danda Pradakshina**: Danda means a stick. It consists of a mixture of walking and prostration. The person needs to take a step and then prostrate (lie flat on the ground like a stick with hands in Namaste position in front of the head). Then get up and repeat the above steps.
- **Anga Pradakshina**: Anga means body. The person needs to prostrate as mentioned above, and roll around the shrine. It is one of the hardest types of Parikrama.

The Parikrama is done inside the mandir and also of trees, rivers, hills e.g., Tulsi plant, Peepal Tree, Narmadaji, Govardhan hill, Vrindavan, Vraj Mandala, Dwadash Madhav parikrama, Tirthraj Prayagji, Ayodhyaji, Girnar, Chitrakoot hill, Varanasi (Kashiji),

<!-- page 60 -->

100

Mathuraji, etc. Let us look at some of them:

Lili Parikrama or Girnar Parikrama: It is a seven-day festival held in Junagadh. The pilgrimage involves a climb of 10,000 steps to reach the top to the sacred Mount Girnar.

Mathura parikrama: The parikrama covers 24 mandirs on the periphery of the old city; the distance covered is 18 km and is done on Akshay Naumi. The parikrama starts and ends at Vishram ghat.

Antargriha Parikrama: The parikrama covers the 20 mandirs within the vicinity of old city, covering 3km with start and end point at Vishram ghat.

Braj Mandal Parikrama: Devotes experience 12 forests and 24 groves over time period of one month. This parikrama is done during "Bhadon" (rainy) month.

Kurukshetra parikrama: 48 kos parikrama of Kurukshetra is circumambulation of over 200 Mahabharata-related and other vedic era tirthas.

Varanasi parikrama: The city older than history has many parikrama routes. Bharne and Krusche describes them as:

*Per the ancient Puranic scriptures, there are about 108 different pilgrimage circuits in Varanasi, each originally associated with different purposes and deities. Many have lost their identities, or have been transformed over time.*

*But around fifty two such journeys still survive to varying degrees, in five sacred territories within the city. One such circular territory symbolizes a sacred journey of the cosmos. It is called the Chaurashikroshi area (Kshetra). It has a circumference of 168 miles. There are 144 mandirs and shrines along this route, the number representing the integration, the integration of the nine planets, four cardinal directions, and four parts of a day. Its cartographic manifestation is called the Kasi Mandala, and is ordered around deities associated with space and time. In each of the eight directions are twelve months of the Hindu year.*

*There are ninety six Shaktis (divine feminine creative power), eight Durgas (the supremely radiant goddess form of Shiv's wife, Parvati), eight Bhairavas (a fierce manifestation of Shiva associated with annihilation), eight Dipakala (guardians of eight Directions) and twenty four Vetals (worshipper of Bhairava and head of spirits, ghouls and vampires) making the total 144.*

*The smaller Panchakrosi Yatra is the most popular of all such pilgrimages. It has a total of 108 sacred sites, the number stemming from the summation of twelve months of the year and the nine planets of Hindu cosmology (Nava Graha). It covers a distance of 55.2 miles, including the Nagar Pradakshina - a coaccumulation of the outer boundary of the urban landscape covering fifteen miles. This journey, believed to provide purification from all types of sins, is divided into five parts, and identified with five spots where pilgrims can stay overnight in rest houses. Pilgrims visit a total of seventy-two mandirs and shrines, representing the integration of nine planets, four cardinal*

---

101

*directions, and the two opposite sides of a day the light versus the dark.*

*Another prominent pilgrimage territory is centred on the Shiva's vow to never forsake Varanasi as his abode. It is called Avimukta (never forsaken territory). The circuit is unique in that it moves four times in clockwise spiral form. It encompasses seventy two sacred sites and images, fifty six dedicated to Shiva, the number symbolizing the summation of seven spinal energy nodes (chakras) and eight cardinal directions, with the inner route involving seven circumambulation around the Visvanatha Mandir.*

*Taken together, the five sacred circuits contain 468 mandirs, shrines and sacred sites, representing the integration of nine planets, thirteen months (twelve plus one intercalary) and the four directions, forming an established unifying order of mythic associations and geographic territories.*

*Additionally, there are pilgrimage routes dedicated to specific purposes and deities, also centred on specific mandirs and spots. The Aditya Yatra, dedicated to the Sun God, contains sixteen destinations. The Ritu yatra dedicated to six seasons and a seventh to all seasons together is associated with six shrines. The Dwarka yatra, dedicated to Krishna, moves around the Dwarkadisha Mandir, connecting seventeen sacred spots. But however large or small, these circuits are by no means hierarchical, the whole believed to be present in each layer of the sacred journey.*

(Rediscovering the Hindu Mandir: The Sacred Architecture and Urbanism of India, 2012 by Vinayak Bharne and Krupali Krusche, Cambridge Scholars)

Narmada parikrama: The Narmada River begins its own journey from the Maikala range, of east central Madhya Pradesh. Emerging on the summit of the plateau of Amarkantak on the north eastern apex of the Satpura range in Rewa, it enters the Arabian sea below Bhuruch, after a total course of 1289 K.M. journey. The sacred Narmada River, the lifeline of Central Bharat, is worshipped as Narmada maiyya (mother). It is the only one which has the tradition of being circumambulated from the source to the sea and back. Narmada parikrama is a formidable spiritual exercise and challenge - an incredible journey of about 2,600 km.

The journey usually starts at the river's source at Amarkantak, goes along its southern banks, all the way to its mouth at Bharuch in Gujarat. At Bharuch, Mithi Talai is the point where the Narmada joins the Arabian Sea. Pilgrims take a motorboat from the southern to the northern end and begin the return journey along its northern bank. There are different type of parikramas, which are as follows:

(1) Mundamal Parikrama: It is considered the most popular Narmada Parikrama among all. A pilgrim can start from any point at the bank of Narmada on foot and come back to the same point after walking around the holy river.

(2) Jalehari Parikrama: In this parikrama, parikramawasi (pilgrim) starts from Amarkantak (originating place of the river Narmada) and walks up to Mithi Talai (Narmada merges here with Sindhu Sagar) and come back to Amarkantak by northern

<!-- page 61 -->

102

side of the river, then goes to the other side of the river and walks up to Kathpore and come back to Amarkantak.

(3) Panchkosi Parikrama: In this Narmada Parikrama, the pilgrim should visit some religious places round Amarkantak on foot. The religious places to visit are Narmada mandir complex, Mai-ki-bagia, Sonemuda, Jaleswar Mahadev mandir, Dhunipani, Bhrigu comomdulu, Kabir chabutra, Kapil dhara, Dugdha dhara, Sambhu dhara, Durga dhara, Baratinala and Pataleswar Mahadev mandir. Another Panchakoshi Parikrama starts from Bandarbhan and ends at Hiranfal.

(4) Khanda Parikrama: There is no binding to complete the journey at one go. Pilgrim can start from any point at the bank of Narmada and continue for some days and may return to home after completion of a part of parikrama. He/she may start parikrama from that point where he left parikrama last time.

(5) Markandeya Parikrama: In this Narmada parikrama, parikramawasi cannot cross not only the holy river Narmada but also the other main rivers that merge with Narmada enroute.

(6) Dandaat Parikrama: This Narmada Parikrama is the toughest journey and parikramawasi should cover the total distance by offering dandawat to Narmada maata.

(7) Hanumant Parikrama: This Parikrama is popular among general tourist because there is no binding to cross the river by boat and the pilgrim can visit the places of spiritual interest according to their choice.

Now people do Narmada parikrama by car. The popularity of this parikrama is growing. Some travelling agencies are conducting this tour from Amarkantak, Omkareshwar, Maheshwar, Bharuch and other big cities situated nearby Narmada. The total distance to cover is about 4000 K.M. and takes about 17 to 20 days to complete the journey. Narmada parikrama by car covers only the shrines near road.

All these parikramas have food outlets, staying places, and all the related services required by a pilgrim in the route. If people visit the local mandir, only the people in neighbourhood will benefit. With 'Parikrama', arthavyavastha of a larger section of the society improves. Author did not come across any study which quantifies the economic benefit but by now we have seen many examples to envisage how when a substantial number of people go for parikrama, there can be economic upliftment of the area.

## F. Tirthayatra (pilgrimage) based Arthavyavastha

*The Matsyapurana has a section "tirtha-mahatmya-pathana-sravana-phalam" (the fruit of reading and listening to the account of the greatness of the place of pilgrimage) which follows some ninety verses of topographical enumeration. The final phalasruti is pronounced by the suta, the bard, whose business is that of the record keeper in puranic literature. The passage reads: "He who hears or listens to this eulogy (anukTrtanam) wholly related in the Matsyapurana, which (eulogy) is meritorious, pure, bestowing*

---

103

*longevity, destroying all sins, such a man becomes a possessor of Sri (i.e., the Devi of Wealth-meaning affluence and well-being in general)."*

- Pilgrimage in the Indian Tradition by Agehananda Bharati, History of Religions, Vol -3, No. 1 (Summer, 1963), pp.125-167

Listening about the greatness of the places of pilgrimage can make one prosperous. For sure the place of pilgrimage has lot of impact on the arthavyavastha.

What makes a place, tirthasthan? Traditionally there are four types of tirthas:

- Daiva tirthas, considered the most auspicious, resulting from the benevolent act of a God;
- Asura tirthas, where a God subdued one or another demon;
- Arsha tirthas, created through the tapas, sadhana and sacrifice of great saints and sages; and
- Manusha tirthas, least auspicious, places of worship established by kings.

Before proceeding further, just a word of caution: The common English expression "place of pilgrimage" is much too restrictive when applied to the sacred places of Bharat. A tirtha, therefore, may be an actual sacred "place", but it may also mean sacred river, sacred mountain, or even sacred forest. Sometimes the word also means a sacred region, although the latter is more appropriately termed kshetra (area or region) rather than tirtha. (Hindu Places of Pilgrimage in India: A Study in Cultural Geography, Religion, 1973 by Surinder Mohan Bhardwaj, Munshiram Manoharlal).

Places of Pilgrimage also define the geography of Bharat. "The innumerable sacred places of the Hindus can be conceived as a system of nodes having varying degrees of religious import. Within this system, some places may be the focal points for pilgrims from the entire vast Bhartiya subcontinent with its variegated cultural mosaic. Other, more modest places may serve as centres of congregation of devotees from the immediate vicinity. Between these two extremes there are sacred places of several intermediate levels. Sacred centres of each "level" have their corresponding pilgrim "fields." The holy places thus generate a gigantic network of religious circulation encompassing the entire Hindu population. Pilgrim "flows" are the connecting links between the Hindu population and its numerous sacred centres. The number of Hindu sanctuaries in Bharat is so large and the practice of pilgrimage so ubiquitous that the whole of India can be regarded as a vast sacred space organized into a system of pilgrimage centres and their fields. Scholars who emphasize the linguistic, regional, and social diversity of Bharat often tend to minimize the integrative role of institutions such as sacred places. More and more social scientists are, however, beginning to be conscious of the indigenous forces of cultural integration." (Hindu Places of Pilgrimage in India: A Study in Cultural Geography, Religion, 1973 by Surinder Mohan Bhardwaj, Munshiram Manoharlal)

The continuous circulation of millions of pilgrims throughout India has forged a

<!-- page 62 -->

national unity of great strength. Swami Chidanand explained, "Pilgrimages have culturally and emotionally unified the Hindus. They have increased the generosity of people. Pilgrims learn and appreciate the many subcultures in the different regions, while also appreciating the overall unity." (Sacred Pilgrimage, 1 May 1997, hinduismtoday.com)

The Mahabharata, in the Tirthayatra section, lists hundreds of holy destinations. Sage Pulastya describes to Bhishma a tour circumambulating all of Bharat in a clockwise fashion, beginning from Pushkara in Rajasthan, then to Somnath and Dwarka in the West, to the Himalayas, across the top of Bharat through Varanasi and Gaya to the mouth of the Ganges in the East, then southward to Kanyakumari, back up the western side of Bharat to Gokarna in Karnataka, and ultimately returning to Pushkara. The existence of this pilgrimage route in ancient times proves, they say, that undivided Bharat was a one culture unified by a one religion.

These yatras did not evolve just for dharmic reasons. Yatra is also an "expression of love for the Motherland" and "expands the geographical consciousness" of the Pilgrim. Every yatra has enormous impact on Arthavyavastha also.

Each yatra has its own area of coverage from where the devotees converge. The Yatra can be broadly classified into three categories:

i) Devotees come from nearby areas during the same period across Bharat e.g., Kanwar yatra, Rath yatra etc.

ii) Devotees come from more than one state e.g., Pandharpur yatra, Girnar yatra.

iii) Devotees come from all over Bharat e.g., Vaishno Devi yatra, Amarnath yatra, Kailash Mansarovar yatra, Sabarimala yatra.

Each one has bumper impact on the arthavyavastha of the area/region. In the following pages we will look at the impact on arthavyavastha by these yatras

**i) Devotees come from nearby areas during the same period across Bharat**

'Kanwar Yatra' is an annual pilgrimage conducted in the month of Shravana during which the devotees carry the sacred waters of Ganga in earthen pitchers and offer the same to Bhagwan Shiv. The Kanwariyas are devotees of Bhagwan Shiv and are also referred to as Bholas. They carry Kanwars - decorated wooden structures containing vessels full of Ganga water on their shoulder - and are hence called Kanwariyas. The yatra is thus called the Kanwar Yatra. Some Kanwars are large, and are often pulled along the route in tractors or jeeps or on carts pulled by men. These vehicles often have loudspeakers playing bhajans. Kanwar Yatra has huge impact on arthavyavastha

In 2020, Kanwar yatra was cancelled due to Wuhan virus and Meerut alone suffered a loss of Rs 200 crore. (उत्तराखंड: चारधाम के बाद अब कांवड़यात्रा से पर्यटन कारोबारियों को झटका, कोई २०० कारोड़ का होगा नुकसान, न्यूज़डेस्क, अमर उजाला, मेरठ 23 June 2020, amarujala.com)

A record 3 crore Kanwarias visited Haridwar in 2018. (Kanwar Yatra concludes, 3 crore pilgrims visit Uttarakhand, 9 August 2018, thestatesman.com)

If every Kanwar spent Rs 500/- only, then the Haridwar would have got 3 Crore X Rs 500 = Rs 15,00,00,00,000/- only. This money would have reached the smallest of traders who operates from road side. And this money would have been spent in the surrounding areas also. Because the path to Haridwar will come through them. The impact it makes on the life of poorest of poor is unbelievable. Imagine the amount and the process of circulation of money in the society. And all this in 15 to 30 days maximum. If government must spend this money one can well imagine the administrative setup government will need and cost incurred on the same. And one can well visualise the corruption in the whole process.

Scheduling of such yatras is also well planned. Rath yatra happens during rainy season and so is the most popular Pandharpur yatra. This is the time when the agricultural activity is at its lowest. Yatra does not harm but pump up the arthavyavastha.

**ii) Devotees come from more than one state.**

There are yatras in which devotees come from more than one state. Some of these yatras are colossal.

**Case Study - VI: Pandharpur Yatra**

Pandharpur, in Solapur, has the mandir of Bhagwan Panduranga (Bhagwan Vitthala). Devotees undertake regular pilgrimage to Pandharpur throughout the year. This pilgrimage is known as 'Wari' and the pilgrims undertaking it are known as 'Warkaris'. (The term Wari has its roots in the original word 'Wari-ri', meaning a group of pilgrims, that regularly undertakes pilgrimage to a holy place). Warkari is there from ancient times and became more popular in the 13th century on the initiative of Saint Dnyaneshwara (Brahmin) and thence onwards, Pandharpur began its ascent as the centre of Warkari tradition. After Dnyaneshwara, other Saints like Tukaram (farmer), Eknath, Namdeo (tailor), Narhari (goldsmith), Savtoba (gardener), Damaji Pant, Gora (potter), Chokha Mela, Janabai and others, through their Abhangas, have exalted the glory of Warkari Sect, Bhagwan Vitthala and Pandharpur. Pandharpur attracts devotees from few other states e.g., Karnataka, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Goa etc, apart from Maharashtra.

A report in Pune Mirror tells us about the importance of this yatra for the region in aarthic terms. "These three months are critical for us. We lost the business we do during Tukaram Beej-Chaitri Wari and now the main Ashadi Wari is gone, too. Other years, in three days, I make Rs 40,000-50,000. That money has been lost this year...a whole year's earning is lost," Gurav told Mirror.

...Kailas Agrawal, says..."I've owned this shop since 1995, but this the first time I opened it without any guarantee of business. Tukaram Beej got over on March 11 and the shop has been shut since. My day's income on this occasion would have been Rs 50,000 a day. Recovering from this loss is going to be difficult."

<!-- page 63 -->

106

Apart from the shopkeepers, the hawkers who travel with the wari are also feeling the pinch as there will be no procession this year to tag along. (Tradition Interrupted by Prachee Kulkarni, 13 June 2020, punemirror.indiatimes.com)

Wari can be undertaken on the 11th day of every month of the Hindu calendar, which divides a month into two fortnights associated with the moon's waxing and waning phases. Thus, there are a total of 12 auspicious occasions in a year to undertake the Wari. Out of this, four occasions are considered particularly auspicious for visiting Pandharpur as a Warkari. These are on the 11th days of the moon's waxing phases in the Hindu months of Ashadh (June), Kartik (November), Maagh (February) and Chaitra (April). These four Waris attract substantial number of devotees to Pandharpur. As per the study of Dhiraj Kumar, Ashadhi Wari attracts 12 lakh pilgrims, Kartiki Wari attracts around 5 lakh pilgrims, while Maghi and Chaitri Waris attract about 2.5 lakh pilgrims each. Kartiki Wari has an added attraction of a large-scale cattle market, that is held along with it.

Any yatra impacts the economy of both, i) the destination and ii) the places covered during the yatra. We will look at the economic impact on both the places.

i) The Destination

Economic impact at Pandharpur, the destination is based on the book 'Importance of Wari (Yatra) in point of Economic view, 2016 by Dhiraj Kumar R. Baad.

Each Warkari coming to Pandharpur for Ashadhi Wari, on an average, spends Rs.913.83/-. Out of this Rs.367.04/- is spent on travel and the remaining Rs.546.79/- are spent on various services availed at Pandharpur. Details are in Table-1. Expenditure incurred by the Warkaris is major source of income for residents of Pandharpur.

**Breakup of the Per Head Expenditure of the Warkaris during Ashadhi Wari (Table-1)**

| Approx. Number of Warkaris | Total Expenditure / Warkaris (₹) | Per Head Average Expenditure on (₹) | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | Travel | Stay | Food | Purchase | Others |
| 12,00,000 | 913.83 | 367.04 | 110.22 | 159.98 | 221.26 | 55.31 |

('Importance of Wari (Yatra) in point of Economic view, 2016 by Dhiraj Kumar R. Baad.)

In Pandharpur, various communities from all over Maharashtra have built their own Mathams for the Warkaris of that particular community, where they can stay at a reasonable cost during the Wari period. There are 500 such large and small Mathams in Pandharpur town. Further, during the Wari periods, many owners of private residential houses also offer rooms to the Warkaris for a brief stay. The number of such private accommodation, in the area surrounding the mandir, is estimated to be around 500.

Apart from all these, there are nearly 300 permanent-type boarding houses in Pandharpur town.

---

Some Warkaris, carry back coconut bought in Pandharpur. During the Ashadhi Wari alone, nearly 3 lakh coconuts.

(4) Children's Readymade Garments: Majority of the Warkaris coming to Pandharpur for the Ashadhi Wari before returning, usually buy readymade clothes for the kids back home. The sellers of these garments put up their roadside stalls.

(5) Sales of Coarse Blankets (Ghongadi) and Solapuri Chuddars: Coarse blanket is a staple item of bedding in many families. In Pandharpur itself, off the Pradakshina

Marg, there is a well-known 'Ghongadi Lane', where some permanent shops deal exclusively in these blankets throughout the year. Many Warkaris buy these blankets from these shops or from the temporary shops, before returning home. Likewise, the nearby Solapur city is reputed for the production of quality Chuddars (cotton bed sheets). Warkaris buy these Chuddars in Pandharpur.

(6) Moneylending: During the Wari period, numerous temporary petty traders and businessmen undertake various income generating activities. Some of them lack sufficient capital for investment. Hence, they borrow from private moneylenders at a rate of 10-15% for the Wari period of 10-15 days. Since the petty traders and businessmen have a profit margin of 25-30%, they can afford to pay such hefty rate of interest. This short-term financing generates incomes of lakhs of Rupees for these moneylenders. Banks and credit cooperatives do not extend such short-term finance.

(7) Promotion of Agriculture: The Wari also promotes the agriculture in the surrounding rural areas in a big way. During the Wari period, demand for agriculture produces such as vegetables, fruits and flowers rises multi-fold. This demand is almost entirely met from the surrounding areas.

This work has, so far, reviewed the economic impact of only the Ashadhi Wari. But there are three more major Waris (Kartiki, Maghi and Chaitri) as well as monthly Waris. A Wari or 'Ekadashi' occurs twice in a month. Hence, there are 24 Waris in a year. Out of these, Chaitri, Ashadhi, Kartiki and Maghi Waris are considered as major Waris. All these occur in the moon's waxing phase. The remaining eight Waris occurring in this phase are considered auspicious days for taking Bhagwan Vitthala's Darshan. The 12 Waris occurring in the moon's waning phase are not considered much auspicious and the attendance of the Warkaris is also significantly less. They do not have much impact. Approximately 60,00,000 Waris visit Pandharpur every year Table 10.

Pandharpur provides employment to thousands of people and generates income in crores because of Wari.

Ashadhi Warkari, on an average, incurs an expenditure of Rs.913.83. After deducting the travelling expenditure the remaining about of Rs.546.79 is spent by him/her in Pandharpur town. Thus, 12 lakh Warkaris collectively spend an amount of Rs.65,61 48,000 in Ashadhi Wari alone. If the annual turnover is five times of this amount, it works out to be Rs.3,28,07,40,000. It generates large scale employment, increases the incomes of the people and changes the economic activities of the local people. This change helps the development of the Pandharpur region's economy.

## ii) Places covered during the yatra

Now let us look at the economic impact on the places covered during the yatra. This part is based on, Impact of Palkhi procession on route region, 2016 by Sudhir D Ingale, Roli Book Distributors.

The yatra has many palkhis. Sant Dnyaneshwar's palkhi leaves from Alandi. Let us look at the route of palkhi of Sant Dnyaseshwar and its economic impact on the route it takes from starting point at Alandi to Pandharpur and back.

Palkhi consists of a long pole of bamboo or steel pipe having curve in middle. A small rectangular wooden platform is hung in its middle. On the pole a silk cloth is tied. Platform is covered with a cushion of makhmal (Velvet). The Padukas are kept on cushioned platform and represent the saints. About eight men carry the palkhi.

Palkhi travels on a fixed route. It starts from Alandi after the Prasthana ceremony on Jyestha Vadya Ashtmi but stays for a night at the home of Saint Dnyaneshwar's maternal grandfathers in Alandi itself. The procession proceeds towards Pandharpur on Navmi. Eighteen days are required to cover the distance of 250 kms and reach Pandharpur. About 2.51 lakh devotees walk with the palkhi procession.

On the way the procession halt at different places for different number of days. The place and number of days it halts is as follows: Pune (2 days), Saswad (2 days), Jejuri (one day), Valhe (one day), Lonand (one or two days), Taradgaon (one day), Phaltan (one or two days), Barad (one day), Natepute (one day) Malshiras (one day), Velapur (one day) Bhandishegaon (one day) and Wakhari (one day).

The duration of stay is a factor of tithis. In between the Jyestha vadya ekadashi and Ashadha Shuddha pratipada (first day of Ashadha) one tithi reduces palkhi haults at Lonand for one day otherwise it is for two days. If the Ashadha suddha comes for two days, the palkhi haults for two days at Phaltan. Otherwise for a day. The procession reaches to Wakhari on the 9th day of bright half of Ashadha. All the other palkhis also gather at the same place on the same day. The palkhi gathering at Wakhari forms a large city of palkhis and dindis. Finally, a mega procession of all palkhis reaches Pandharpur on Ashadha Shuddha Dashmi (10th day of Ashadha).

The return journey of Sant Dnyaneshwar palkhi procession begins on full moon day in the afternoon. Palkhi stays at Wakhari, Velapur, Natepute, Phaltan, Padegaon, Valhe Saswad, Hadapsar and Pune. The palkhi reaches Alandi on the dark dashmi. It takes 10 days to cover the distance. The daily average distance covered by the palkhi is about 25 kms. The lowest distance covered by the palkhi procession is 4 kms from Pandharpur to Wakhari. While longest distance covered is 40 kms from Natepute to Phaltan.

The speed of the return journey is slightly more than the journey from Alandi to Pandharpur. Hence the days required to cover the distance is less than the journey to Pandharpur. In Alandi the presence of all dindis with veena at Hajeri Maruti mandir is expected at the end of the procession. 32 days are required to complete the yatra from start to end.

Accommodation facilities in the procession are made available by the dindi organizers. A dindi is a group of devotees of one caste or village who are part of a larger palkhi going on pilgrimage. First five dindis in the front are as old as palkhi procession itself and are positioned very close to the palkhi in the procession. These dindis take night hault on "Palkhi Tal" in tents, while middle dindis have their traditional halting places such as in the private houses, school buildings, godowns, temples, Samaj Mandirs etc. New dindis stay in tent facilities on open ground in nearby areas of town. Local people extend all possible co-operation for the accommodation of the pilgrims.

Many pilgrims prefer to stay in hotels. There are seventeen good hotels (lodges) in Alandi and fifteen in Pandharpur while there are eight lodges in Saswad, fifteen at Jejuri, four at Lonand, nine at Phaltan, four at Natepurte, five at Malshiras and two at Velapur. The rate per head per day is Rs. 50 and per room charge is Rs. 150 to 160 per day. Recently the Madhya Pradesh state government has constructed Bhakta Nivas at Gopalpur road Pandharpur. It is used mainly by the pilgrims of Madhya Pradesh with concessional rates (Table - 11).

### iii) Devotees come from all over Bharat

For some yatras devotees come from all over Bharat.

### Case Study - VII: Amarnath Yatra

Amarnath Shrine, the holy cave is the abode of Bhagwan Shiv. Situated in a narrow gorge at the farther end of Lidder Valley, in Jammu & Kashmir. Amarnath Shrine stands at 3,888 meters, 46 Km from Pahalgam and 14 Kms from Baltal. Often Islamic Terrorist kill Hindu pilgrimage on this route. Ironically, it is the Muslims who make a living out of this yatra. Sabrang India reports that -

2021 marks the third successive season when the yatra has been cancelled - in 2019, it was because of security concerns surrounding the government's decision to scrap Article 370, and Covid has been to blame in the two subsequent years. It is a knock that has left Sonmarg's ghodawallahs - approximately 250 in number - struggling.

"Three years ago, during the yatra time, we used to earn Rs 5,000 a day and, for the rest of the year, especially the summer, tourists flocked to the area. However, now we are not even making Rs 2,000 a month and are in heavy debt. There are some days when we have nothing to eat," Bhatt said. Farooq Ahmed Bhatt (40), is a ghodawallah (horse porter) of Sonmarg, Kashmir. (No Amarnath Yatra for 3 yrs: Sonmarg horses are idle, their owners jobless and 'in huge debt', Ananya Bhardwaj, 20 July, 2021, The Print.in)

From walking sticks to puja items to Kashmiri shawls, local Muslims earn handsome money during the yatra period. Business of walking sticks touches nearly Rs 40 lakh during the Amarnath yatra. According to Mohammad Ashraf and Nazir Ahmed Lone, over 200 people are involved in preparing and selling these sticks to the pilgrims. On an average, each of them sells 1,000 sticks during the yatra period at a cost of Rs 20 per stick. 200 persons sell 2,00,000 sticks – i.e., Rs 40 lakh per season. Almost all pilgrims who prefer to walk on foot, purchase walking sticks. Local taxi operators also earn handsomely during the yatra period because no taxi is allowed beyond Pahalgam so pilgrims have to travel in local taxis to reach the Chandanwari base camp. (Local residents cash in on Amarnath yatra, 10 July 2017, tribuneindia.com)

Amarnath Yatra is source of livelihood for a wide cross section of people since inception. Following is a news item from 2013.

Sikandar Butshikan spent years destroying our mandirs in Jammu & Kashmir but still could not destroy all of them because our Mandirs are in many forms. The Hindus who were forcefully converted to Islam, today oppose Amarnath Yatra and still make a

living out of Amarnath Yatra. What could be more potent example of Mandir based or Pilgrimage based arthavyavastha.

### G. Mela (fair) based Arthavyavastha

*The market ran during Hardwar's spring bathing festival, which provided a definite time for the market every year and allowed the caravans to time their departures appropriately. This trade route was so flexible and the merchants were so determined because the trade was immensely lucrative and would always bring a handsome profit. Among the goods on this route, Raper mentions dry fruits, shawls, ivory and brass manufactures, rock salt, and woollen cloth; Bayly also mentions gold, musk, and Persian carpet dyes. Bayly particularly stresses the shawls, which he claims carried immense symbolic value. He describes the Kashmir shawl as the "universal symbol of aristocracy in the Indo-Persian world" and even contends that the market was primarily a shawl mart. Accounts of the fair in the early 1800s certainly mention shawls but give far greater attention to livestock, which seems to have been the fair's most important feature. For many years, the Hardwar fair was the largest horse fair in India, and one of the regular visitors was the East India Company, which sent representatives to buy cavalry remounts. There were also camels, cattle, and elephants, as well as exotic animals-felines from domestic cats to tigers, "dogs, bears, monkeys, birds, and deer of every description", and even a wild ass from the Rann of Kutch. The exotic animals would have been brought only for sale, but the horses, camels, and other beasts of burden not only were sold as merchandise but also carried merchants and their goods to the fair. After the fair, the merchants could return home, or they could continue down the Ganges into the Doab, to dispose of any unsold livestock or merchandise. Capital and banking were clearly present at the fair, since these are essential perquisites for long-distance trade, & a host of bankers & moneylenders sent agents to Hardwar to provide this.*

\- God's Gateway, 2009 by James Lochtefeld, Oxford University Press

Fairs are held all over the world, but the number of fairs held in Bharat is quite large. Most of these fairs are dharmic. They may be national, regional, or local. Kumbh is a national fair; the Garh Mukteshwar fair is regional, and then there are local fairs.

### Case Study - VIII: Kumbh Mela

In Bharat, the most important among the national fairs is the Kumbh fair. It is bigger than Olympics in terms of participation. In February 1989, the Government had estimated that at least one and a half crore people would take bath during the Prayag Kumbh, but the number exceeded four crore. Only a line mentioning the date and place of this fair in the Hindu calendar is indication enough of the holding of the fair. Thousands of foreigners attend the fair only to have a peep into the Hindu customs, traditions and philosophy.

Hindu history, talks about amrit manthan. When, finally, the pitcher of nectar appeared

<!-- page 70 -->

a few drops of nectar spilled over and fell at four places. These four places are sacred spots where the Kumbh fair is held, viz. Haridwar, Prayag, Ujjain and Nasik. Since Purna Kumbh is a 12-yearly fair, Kumbh is held at each of the four places every three years. At Haridwar and Prayag, between two Purna Kumbh fairs, the Ardh Kumbh is also held every six years.

Our forefathers had fixed different timings for the Kumbh fairs at the said four places on the basis of astronomical calculations. These timings are being scrupulously observed even today. Astrologers have divided planetary bodies into twelve categories, namely, (1) Aries, (2) Taurus, (3) Gemini, (4) Cancer, (5) Leo, (6) Virgo, (7) Libra, (8) Scorpio, (9) Sagittarius, (10) Capricorn, (11) Aquarius and (12) Pisces. Various planets like Mercury, Saturn, Earth, Moon, Jupiter etc. which revolve around the Sun take a definite time to complete a circuit. To move from one zodiac sign to another, the Sun takes approximately one month, the Moon two and a half days, Jupiter about one year, and so on.

These beneficial planetary influences are more pronounced on water which sustains it for a long time. This is why the Kumbh fair is held in close proximity of rivers (Table-1).

Holiest days for bath at the four Kumbhs:

Prayag Kumbh: Makar Sankranti, Mauni Amavasya, and Vasant Panchami.

Haridwar Kumbh: Shivratri, Chaitra Amavasya and Maish Sankranti.

Nasik: Shravan Amavasya, Singh Sankranti, Shravan Purnima and Bhadra Krishna Ekadashi.

Ujjain: Maish Sankranti, Vaishakh Amavasya and Vaishakh Purnima

The Mela is convocation of scholars and saints who sojourn here to engage in mutual discussion on issues related to this world and the next. Primarily an assembly of sadhus and mahatmas, the Kumbh Mela in its present form was further institutionalised by Adi Shankaracharya. He classified the Hindu ascetics into ten sects and ordained the heads of these sects to assemble regularly at the Kumbh Mela, not only for maintaining mutual contact among themselves but also for exchanging experiences in their divine quest, to review the existing state of society, for suggesting reforms, if required.

Hiuen Tsang described the mela which he had seen for himself in 644 CE and said:

*The entire mela was organised in an area of five miles and about five lakhs of people had gathered before King Harshyanardhana of Thaneshwar reached the mela. There was a decorated square barricading of 1,000 steps of bamboos where the jewels, gold and silver were stored for distribution. About 100 temporary houses were constructed for shelter of pilgrims. The King distributed his entire treasury, his belongings, costly jewels and even his royal garments. Thereafter he asked his sister to provide him clothes.*

**2. The Financial boost that modern corporates derive out of mela.**

Kumbh Mela is exploited by the corporates as a big business opportunity.
